1:
Everything in the verse turns on who the many were and how they are being treated. Gill argues they cannot be the authentic historians of evangelical facts: two men cannot with any propriety be called many, and Luke would hardly insinuate a deficiency in them. Wesley agrees in a line, that Matthew and Mark are not meant and John did not write so early. Ellicott takes the verse as evidence that written documents professing to give the Gospel history already existed when Luke wrote, and allows that the many may have included the other evangelists though we cannot say. Robertson notes how uncommon the opening word is, occurring here alone in the New Testament though ordinary in literary Attic; and he observes that the verb rendered taken in hand is the one Hippocrates and Galen use in the introductions to their medical works, common in the papyri for simply undertaking a thing, with no suggestion of blame.

Whether a reproach is nevertheless implied divides the bench. Ellicott hears no tone of disparagement at all — the writer simply feels his predecessors have not exhausted the subject and that his own inquiries enable him to add something. Robertson reads it the same way and adds that the motive is universal, every author being moved by the sense that there is still room for his book. Chrysostom sees the writer refusing to rest on his own authority at all: so far was the Evangelist from being content with his single testimony that he refers the whole to the apostles, seeking from them a confirmation of his words, since our chief ground for believing a thing is that we derive it from those who actually saw. Calvin is less easy. Though Luke deals gently with those who had written before him, he does not altogether approve their labours: he does not say they wrote of matters they were imperfectly acquainted with, but by laying claim to certainty he modestly denies their title to full and unshaken confidence. Calvin thinks they may have erred more from want of consideration than from malice, so that no fierceness of attack was called for, and that these were little more than historical sketches, harmless at the time, which if not promptly counteracted would afterwards have done serious injury to the faith. Henry keeps the charitable reading and draws a rule from it: the labours of others in the gospel of Christ, if faithful and honest, we ought to commend and encourage rather than despise, though chargeable with many deficiencies, and their service must not be reckoned to supersede ours but rather to quicken it.

About the writer himself the record is thin, and Clarke lays out what there is. Lardner took Luke for a Jew by birth, Michaelis for a Gentile, arguing from the way Paul distinguishes those of the circumcision from Lucas and Demas; some ancients and some judicious moderns make him one of the two who walked to Emmaus, the companion Cleopas is not named beside; and all the ancients of repute agree that he was a physician. The tradition that he was also a painter of the Virgin Clarke dismisses as fabulous, since no writer attributes the skill to him before Nicephorus in the fourteenth century. Barnes reaches the same conclusion about the Emmaus story from the text itself, since Luke does not profess to have been an eyewitness; he reports the uniform testimony of the fathers that Luke was the companion of Paul, and their claim that what he set down was in effect the gospel Paul preached. On the last participle Robertson notes a real ambiguity, the word meaning fully persuaded when used of persons and completed when used of things, and Luke is speaking of matters. Ellicott renders it accomplished among us; Calvin says it denotes things fully ascertained, which do not admit of doubt.
2:
Ellicott finds something noticeable in the candour with which the writer disclaims the character of an eyewitness, and notes that the verb rendered delivered is Paul's word for what he received concerning the Supper and the Resurrection — almost a technical term for the oral teaching that carried an outline of the Lord's life. Robertson will not let the modern sense intrude: tradition has come to carry a suggestion of unreliability with us, but the handing down here was dependable, not mere wives' fables, and both written and oral sources lay open to Luke. He notes that the word for eyewitnesses means seeing with one's own eyes, occurs here only in the New Testament, and belongs to the medical vocabulary, while the word for ministers means under-rowers or attendants. Ellicott glosses that one as something between a slave and a minister, and takes the word for the message in its general Pauline sense as equivalent to the gospel rather than the higher personal meaning it acquired later in John — a reading Clarke defends explicitly, since no inspired penman uses the term of Christ himself except John. Gill identifies the witnesses as the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples, and Robertson observes that from the beginning must mean the beginning of the ministry, which is why the childhood narratives that follow go behind it: such matters would not have formed part of the traditional preaching.

On the writer's own qualification the bench agrees more than usual, and turns it into a doctrine of inspiration. Barnes renders the phrase having exactly traced everything from the first, and draws two conclusions: that God does not set aside our natural faculties, since no man is convinced of the truth of religion who does not investigate; and that Luke's inspiration was consistent with using them, God presiding over them and keeping him from error. Clarke says the same in his own terms, that the gift of the Spirit was never designed to set aside the powers God has already endued the soul with, these being as truly his gifts as the Spirit is; Luke set himself by impartial inquiry to find the whole truth, and the Spirit so directed it that he was preserved from every particle of error. Calvin takes the verb as a metaphor from those who tread in another's footsteps so that nothing may escape them, and recalls Demosthenes using it of an investigation so diligent that the man perceived all that was done as well as if he had been a spectator. Robertson reports Cadbury's objection that the word need not imply research at all, and answers that Luke is at least claiming fulness of knowledge before he began.

What order he claims is a smaller question with a sharp edge. Wesley says Luke describes in order of time, the acts of Christ and then of the apostles, but in many smaller circumstances does not observe it. Barnes denies exact chronology is meant at all, since that is not how the book is written, and takes the word to mean distinctly, in opposition to the confused and broken accounts mentioned before. Ellicott allows a distinct aim at chronological arrangement but cautions that where Luke's order varies from the other Gospels it does not follow that his is the true one, an avowed compiler being at some disadvantage there. Of the man addressed, Barnes argues the title denotes rank or office rather than character, being given elsewhere only to Felix and Festus, and draws from that the propriety of addressing officials by their customary titles even where the character is unworthy. Robertson closes on the last word, from a verb meaning to totter with the negative prefixed: Luke promises a narrative that will not slip, so that Theophilus shall know the faith he has embraced rests on an impregnable historical foundation.
5:
Calvin explains the order with an image: Luke begins with John the Baptist as a man who was going to speak about the daylight would commence with the dawn. The other evangelists bring him forward already discharging his office, whereas Luke secures our respect for him while he is yet unborn, so that he might afterwards be heard with the more profound veneration when he came forth to exhibit the glory of Christ. Chrysostom finds a graded design in the pairing: the historian relates one marvellous event before another, the less before the greater, for since a virgin was about to become a mother it had been fore-ordained that the old should first conceive. Henry adds what the choice gains: the two preceding evangelists began with John's baptism, but this one, designing a fuller account of the Saviour's birth, gives the same for his forerunner, the morning star to the Sun of righteousness.

The name of the king raises the chapter's first dispute. Henry takes the note of time as proof that the sceptre was quite departed from Judah and that now was the moment for Shiloh to come, the family of David being sunk at the very point when it was to rise again in the Messiah; and he draws the comfort out, that none ought to despair of the reviving of religion even when civil liberties are lost: Israel enslaved, and yet then comes the glory of Israel. Clarke argues the same from Herod's descent, an Idumean who professed himself a proselyte but regarded no religion further than it served his ambition, so that for the first time the throne of Judah was filled by a man not of Jewish extraction. Calvin flatly denies the inference. Those who speak so do not correctly understand the patriarch's prophecy, which promises the Messiah not merely after royal authority had been taken from the Jews but after it had been removed from the tribe of Judah; the sceptre did not break because Herod was foreign, but because whatever relics of rank still lingered in that tribe were carried off by his robbery — the Sanhedrim, chosen out of the family of David, having lasted until Herod avenged an old condemnation by a shocking slaughter of the judges. Gill keeps to the plain fact that Herod held all Judea by deputation from the emperor, and that at his death it was divided among his sons.

Robertson marks the seam in the Greek itself. The verb is not the ordinary word for was but one meaning there arose, and with it the literary polish of the preface disappears: to the end of the second chapter we have the most Hebraistic passage in Luke's writings, resting plainly on documents or notes of oral tradition. He tells the story throughout from Mary's standpoint as Matthew tells his from Joseph's. Robertson counts twenty-four courses, Abijah the eighth, each serving from sabbath to sabbath twice a year, and quotes Plummer that to be a priest and married to a priest's daughter was a double distinction. Ellicott notes a complication: only four courses are named as returning from the Captivity and Abijah is not among them, though the name reappears in later lists, so the twenty-four were soon reorganised. Since priests might marry outside their own caste within limits, he thinks priestly descent on both sides worth the notice, and observes that Elisabeth's name in its Hebrew form had belonged to Aaron's own wife. Clarke makes the descent nobility, since by both parents John came of the family of Amram, and turns the dating itself into evidence: anyone alive when the Gospel was published might have applied to the families named, and in all that age no man arose to call the account in question. Wesley notes only that each course served seven days, every priest's part being assigned him by lot.
6:
The commendation is unusually full, and Gill first fixes where it is registered: not as the Pharisees, righteous only before men, but in the sight of God, who sees the heart and whose judgment is according to truth — and therefore, he adds, not justified by the deeds of the law, but made righteous through the righteousness of Christ, as the saints before his coming were as truly as those after it. God beheld them in his Son, clothed with the righteousness he had engaged to bring in. Clarke divides the praise between two lives: upright and holy in all their outward conduct in civil affairs, and before God possessing the spirit of the religion they professed, so that they were as conscientious in their religious duties as in their neighbourly ones — what a sacred pair, he exclaims, who made their duty to God, to their neighbour, and to themselves walk constantly hand in hand. Robertson hears an Old Testament conception in the very idiom, and borrows Ragg's phrase for the group this couple belongs to, the noblest product of Old Testament education, privileged to see with clear eyes the dawn of the New Testament revelation.

The two nouns are read alike by nearly everyone. Ellicott takes the first to cover all the moral laws of the Pentateuch and the second its outward and ceremonial rules; Wesley renders them moral commandments and ceremonial ordinances and breaks off into prayer that our own obedience might be as sincere and universal; Clarke makes the same division, the first perhaps the decalogue and the second the judicial and ceremonial precepts delivered after it. Calvin insists the order between the two halves of the verse matters more than the division within one of them. Our first study ought to be to approve ourselves to God, who chiefly requires a sincere heart and a pure conscience, so that whoever regulates his outward life by obedience while neglecting uprightness of heart has inverted the sequence; obedience occupies the second rank, and there no man may frame for himself a new form of righteousness unsupported by the Word. He notes too that hypocrites are often very exact in ceremonies, but lay hold on naked and empty ones, where sincere worshippers observe the same rites in a spiritual manner.

Then Calvin raises the obvious objection against himself. If Zacharias and Elisabeth were blameless in keeping the law, they had no need of the grace of Christ, since a full observance of the law brings life and leaves no guilt behind. His answer is that such magnificent commendations must be taken with an exception, God dealing with his servants according to a covenant whose first clause is free reconciliation and daily pardon: their pious endeavours fall far short of perfection, so the righteousness commended in them rests on his forbearance in not reckoning their remaining unrighteousness. He will not accept the shorter solution that Luke means only that they were righteous by faith, calling that a torturing of the words which states a part of the truth and not the whole. On the childlessness Gill is careful that no inference be drawn against them, since it was no judgment for sin and had been the lot of righteous pairs before — Abraham and Sarah, Manoah and his wife, Elkanah and Hannah. Calvin counts two hindrances rather than one, barrenness in the prime of life and now an age which of itself shuts up the womb, so that God gives a twofold exhibition of power to testify that the Prophet was sent by himself. Clarke sets the three annunciations side by side, God foretelling Isaac's birth, the angel of the Lord John's, and Gabriel Christ's; Robertson prefers Wycliff's rendering of the last clause, that they had gone far in their days.
8:
Gill is careful about the status of the lot: it was not an original settled law of God but a custom which in process of time, through the sheer number of the priests, took place and prevailed. Clarke reports the same from the Talmud, that the priests divided the different functions of the sacerdotal office among themselves by lot, and that the decision on this occasion fell to Zacharias to burn the incense in the holy place. Ellicott explains the two layers — the order of the courses settled by rotation, the distribution of functions within the week by lot — and then disposes of an old hope built on it. Attempts have been made to fix the precise date of these events, and so of the Nativity, by reckoning back from the destruction of the Temple, when the course of Joiarib is known to have been ministering on the ninth day of Ab; but all such calculations, he says, are necessarily more or less precarious. Robertson glosses the verb literally as he obtained the lot, an old word in use from Homer onward, and notes what the outcome meant: only once in a lifetime did a priest obtain the lot of entering the sanctuary and burning incense on the golden altar, the fortunate lot being a white stone.

What follows from that is a description of a single morning. Robertson borrows Vincent's account of the ritual — the priests ascending the steps to the Holy Place, spreading the coals on the golden altar and arranging the incense, until the officiating priest was left alone within to await the president's signal to burn it — and observes that this was probably the moment when the angel appeared. He quotes Ragg for the human side of it: this was the great moment of Zacharias's life, and his heart was no doubt alert for the supernatural. Ellicott says why the office was the most distinctive of all priestly acts, since the incense symbolised the presenting of the people's prayers with the priest's own joined to them, so that at such a moment every hope of a man who looked for the Christ as the consolation of Israel would gather itself into one great intercession. Clarke adds the shadow across the scene: this was the temple where God used to manifest his presence, though long before this time he had forsaken it, and yet on this occasion the angel of his presence visited it again.

Calvin uses the arrangement to teach mediation. The twice-daily incense was expressly enjoined by the law of God, while the courses were David's ordering, and David ordained nothing the law had not prescribed, only pointing out a plan by which each family might take its turn at the service God had commanded. The word Luke uses here means the sanctuary proper, which deserves attention, since it can elsewhere take in the outer court; Zacharias goes where none but priests were permitted, and the people stand at a great distance, the altar of sacrifice intervening between them and the altar of incense. Whenever a priest entered the holy place he went as it were into the presence of God, to stand between him and the people; and it was the Lord's will to have this impressed on them, that no mortal is allowed access to heaven without a priest going before, and that while men live on earth they come to the heavenly throne acceptably only in the person of the Mediator. Since two might never discharge the office of intercession at once, the classes were so arranged that one priest entered alone. And the design of the incense itself, Calvin says, was to remind believers that the sweet savour of their prayers does not ascend to heaven except through the sacrifice of that Mediator.
10:
Gill places the crowd exactly, in the court of the Israelites while Zacharias was within the holy place, and infers from its size that this may well have been a sabbath, since on an ordinary day only the priests and Levites of the course, the stationary men who represented the people, and some of the more devout would have been there, whereas here is the whole multitude. Wesley says this was the constant practice of the pious Jews, and the foundation of that elegant figure by which prayer is so often compared in Scripture to incense, ordained perhaps to intimate how acceptable the prayer that accompanied it was. Clarke draws the correspondence tighter: the incense was itself an emblem of the prayers of God's people, so that while the priest performs the rite the people are employed in the thing signified — happy the people, he adds, who attend to the spirit as well as the letter of every divine institution. He notes that incense was burnt morning and evening, and that the evangelist does not say which, though probably the morning. Robertson finds the whole posture in one periphrastic imperfect, the crowd at prayer outside while the clouds of incense rose within.

Chrysostom keeps both actions in one frame: Zacharias had entered the temple to offer prayers for all men, interceding between God and man, and it was there he saw an angel standing. Robertson notes that the verb for appeared is the very form Paul uses of the resurrection appearances, and refuses the softening options — we must choose, with Plummer, between admitting an objective appearance and calling the whole a myth. Ellicott explains why the position mattered. The altar of incense stood immediately before the veil dividing the outer sanctuary from the Holy of Holies, of shittim wood overlaid with gold, both symbols of incorruption, and so closely connected with the inner chamber that the writer to the Hebrews seems to reckon it as belonging there; it symbolised the nearest approach to God then possible for any but the high priest on the day of Atonement. Clarke finds every circumstance significant — that an angel should appear at all, when neither prophecy nor angelic ministry had been vouchsafed for some four hundred years; that he was sent to a priest, whose office pointed out the Son of God until he came; that it happened at Jerusalem rather than the hill country where the priests lived, so that there should be witnesses; and that it fell at the solemn hour of public prayer.

Whose prayer was heard is a real question, and Augustine presses it. It is not likely that Zacharias, offering sacrifice for the redemption of the people, would neglect the public petitions in order to pray, an old man with an old wife, that he might have children; and no one prays for what he despairs of obtaining — as he had so despaired that he would not believe the promise even from an angel. The words must therefore be understood of the people; and since their salvation and the putting away of their sins was to be through Christ, a son is announced to Zacharias because that son was ordained to be Christ's forerunner. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the other end of the temple, since we may well believe that the prayers of the crowd, no less than the priest's, turned toward the manifestation of the kingdom, and that in it stood the aged Simeon and Anna the prophetess and many others who waited for redemption in Jerusalem — so that what followed was the answer to their prayers. Gill identifies the messenger as Gabriel, the same who had appeared to Daniel about the evening oblation nearly five hundred years before, with an account of the time of the Messiah's coming in his mouth.
12:
Gill accounts for the terror by rarity: such appearances were not now so common as formerly, and even when they were more usual they generally had this effect on the minds of good men. Ellicott says the same of the man's own experience, that in all the long years of his ministration he had seen no such manifestation, and guesses at the form from the analogy of other angelic appearances — a young man clothed in white linen or in bright apparel, a kind of transfigured Levite. Clarke supplies a reason nearer the bone: Zacharias feared that this heavenly messenger had come to denounce the judgments of God against a faithless and disobedient people who had too long and too well merited them. Wesley finds a mercy in the ordinary invisibility of such servants, since a man accustomed to converse with God was here thrown into consternation, nature not being able to sustain the sight.

Calvin turns the fear into a doctrine and then withdraws its sting. God does not appear to his servants for the purpose of terrifying them, yet it is advantageous and even necessary that they be struck with awe, so that amid their agitation they learn to give God the glory due to his name. His presence humbles the pride of the flesh, which is naturally so insolent that men never submit until overcome by force; whence Calvin infers that it is only when they have withdrawn from his presence that they indulge in self-flattery, since anyone with God before his eyes as Judge would at once fall prostrate. If this befell Zacharias at the sight of an angel, who is but a spark of the Divine light, what shall become of us if the majesty of God overwhelms us with its brightness? But the glory of God is not so appalling to the saints as to swallow them up, only to cast them down from a foolish confidence; and as soon as he has abased the pride of the flesh in those who believe, he stretches out his hand to raise them up, dealing otherwise with the reprobate, who at his tribunal are overwhelmed with despair. They are greatly mistaken, Calvin adds, who hide themselves from the face of God in order to enjoy peace.

Which prayer was heard is disputed, and the answers spread across the whole range. Clarke will have both: the words refer to the prayers Zacharias had offered for a son and to those for the deliverance of Israel, and they are all heard — from which he draws the comfort that fervent prayers not immediately answered are not lost but registered in heaven, to be answered in the best time. Ellicott takes the opposite line, that the hope of a son had died out long before and the prayer implied is that the Kingdom of God might come, so that praying for this the man receives more than he asks. Robertson thinks it probably was the prayer for a son, in spite of Elisabeth's great age, though he allows the Messianic redemption as possible. Calvin agrees it is hardly probable that Zacharias prayed then for a child he had despaired of, and settles for the reading that a prayer long poured out was at length heard — adding that the desire of children, if not excessive, is consistent with piety, Scripture assigning it no low place among the blessings of God. On the name he holds it was given to heighten the authority of the office: it commends not the grace bestowed on the man privately but the grace his mission would bring to all, and its weight is increased by its date, since God inscribed this token of favour on him before he was born.
14:
Calvin will not let the promised joy shrink to a nursery. The angel describes a gladness greater than the birth of a child could give, since Zacharias was to have such a son as he had not ventured to wish; and it would not be domestic joy, confined within private walls, but shared by strangers, a son born not to Zacharias only but as Teacher and Prophet of the whole people. He turns sharply on those who have made the verse a warrant for keeping the Baptist's birthday with processions and dancing and licence, since the angel restricts his commendation to the joy godly men would take in the man's instruction. Ellicott hears in the same clause an echo of the priest's own petition: he had been seeking the joy of many rather than his own, and now the one was to be fruitful in the other. Gill lists what the joy would rest on: that this son should be the prophet of the Highest, prepare the Lord's ways, and give knowledge of salvation. Robertson notes that the second noun is a word for extreme exultation.

The prohibition is a matter of lexicography, and Barnes takes the trouble to disarm a false inference. The wine commonly drunk in Judea was a light wine, often no stronger than cider, and the common drink of every class; its use was forbidden to the Nazarite alone. As for the second term, he insists it cannot mean strong drink in our sense, since distilled spirits were not then known, the art having been discovered by an Arabian chemist centuries later — and distilled liquors are not used by Arabians at all, who banished them as if sensible of their pernicious influence, while Europe and America are where the poison has ruined millions. Clarke traces the word to the Hebrew verb meaning to inebriate, quotes Jerome that any inebriating liquor is called sicera whether made of corn, apples, honey, or dates, and derives our own cyder from it. Ellicott sets the vow in its line of descent — a Nazarite for life, the representative of the separated form of a consecrated life, what Samson had been and probably Samuel — and reads the abstinence as making room for something: the absence of the lower stimulation implied a capacity for the higher enthusiasm which is the gift of God. Robertson puts that contrast in a phrase, the Holy Spirit set over against the physical excitement of strong drink.

What the greatness consists in is the last question. Gill answers that it was not greatness of birth and blood or of worldly riches, but of gifts and grace, of work and office and usefulness. Calvin says the words are meant less to extol eminent virtues than to proclaim a glorious office, as Christ's saying about the greatest born of women refers less to holiness of life than to ministry; the abstinence itself was no singular virtue but a visible token by which the world might acknowledge a lifelong Nazarite. From which he refuses the obvious application: we must not imagine that the worship of God consists in abstaining from wine, as apish copyists pick some part of the fathers' actions for imitation — let all practise temperance, and let those who have no wine endure the want contentedly. On the filling he is equally restrained, taking it to convey nothing more than a pre-eminent abundance of the Spirit's gifts, since to Christ alone was the Spirit given without measure. Clarke reports a reading followed by one manuscript, two versions and four of the primitive fathers which puts the filling in the womb rather than from it, and asks whether it did not take place at the salutation of the Virgin. Wesley makes the two halves one thing: exemplary in self-denial, and so much the more filled with the Holy Ghost.
16:
Ellicott hears where the sentence comes from: the opening words of the message of the New Covenant spring out of the closing words of the last of the prophets, and point to that revival of the Elijah ministry which the next verse announces outright. Barnes glosses the turning simply as repentance, a calling of men from their sins to seek the Lord their God. Gill holds the prediction to have been verified precisely because the word is many and not all — great multitudes flocked to John, attended his ministry and submitted to his baptism, while some slighted his preaching and rejected it. Calvin reads a darker fact out of the same word. Those in whom conversion could take place must have been apostates, so the verse shows how dissolute the Church then was, corrupt doctrine and depraved morals and disorderly government making it next to a miracle that a very few continued in godliness; and if the ancient Church could be so far gone, then it is a frivolous pretext by which the Papists defend their own superstitions when they say the Church cannot err.

The promise also seems to give a man more than a man can do, and Calvin puts the difficulty plainly: conversion renews men to spiritual life and is therefore not only God's own work but a greater one than the creation of men, so that a minister credited with it would be made equal to God the Creator. His answer is that when the Lord bestows such praise on the outward doctrine he does not separate it from the secret influence of his Spirit, operating through the men whose services he employs, so that a voice which by itself would spend itself uselessly in the air becomes an efficacious instrument. Ministers are nothing more than the hand of God, and both things are asserted in this one clause. Calvin adds a proof from the record itself: it plainly does not lie in the minister's power to bring men back, since John did not indiscriminately bring all back, as he unquestionably would have done had everything yielded to his wish. Wesley takes the practical encouragement — none need be ashamed of preaching like John the Baptist.

Whom he goes before is left grammatically open, and the bench closes it the same way by three routes. Barnes says the connection leads us to suppose the pronoun refers to the Lord their God in the previous verse, and that if so it follows that the Messiah was the Lord God of Israel. Robertson agrees it must be the Lord their God, since the Messiah has not yet been mentioned, though John was in fact to be his forerunner. Calvin makes the silence itself the argument: the angel names no Christ here but declares John the usher and standard-bearer of the eternal God, and from that we learn the eternal divinity of Christ. On the Elijah clause Calvin warns against indulging a dream like that of Pythagoras, as though the prophet's soul had passed into John's body, when what is meant is that the same Spirit who acted efficaciously in Elijah exerted a like power in the Baptist; Robertson notes that John himself will deny being Elijah in person, as they expected, while Jesus will call him Elijah in spirit. Clarke traces the resemblance to the austere manner of life and the zeal that reproved even princes, and reads the turning of hearts as a figure in which the patriarchs, alienated from their children by unbelief, are brought to look on them again with delight — though some, he reports, take the fathers for the Jews and the children for the Gentiles. Robertson prefers a plainer sense, that paternal love had died out and its revival in the home is among the first results of conversion.
18:
Chrysostom states the two grounds of the doubt as the man himself would have felt them: his own age and his wife's barrenness, an unseasonable time of life and an ill-suited nature, the planter infirm and the soil barren. He reports at once that some think the objection unpardonable in a priest, since when God declares anything it becomes us to receive it in faith, and disputes of this kind are the mark of a rebellious spirit. Gill sharpens the ingratitude — that after such an appearance, in such a place, and with these things given as the return of his own prayer, he still wanted a sign, as the Jews were generally desirous of doing, and as the father of them had done in much the same language. Robertson glosses the question as according to what, and puts it plainly: it was too good to be true, so the man who had prayed for the blessing turned sceptical when it came, like the disciples in the house of Mary who would not believe Peter stood at the door. Barnes allows the thing was improbable and evidence natural to desire, but holds that the testimony of an angel in such a place should have been proof enough, and that men are simply slow to believe heavenly messengers.

Calvin raises the harder question, which is not why Zacharias doubted but why he alone was punished for it. Abraham brought forward his old age in the same way, and his faith is so highly applauded that Paul says he considered not his own body now dead nor yet the deadness of Sarah's womb. Gideon was not blamed for asking a sign twice. Mary's own objection follows a few verses later, and the angel passes it over as if it contained nothing wrong. If the words alone are weighed, Calvin concedes, either all of them were equally to blame or Zacharias did nothing wrong. His answer is that words and actions must be judged from the state of the heart, and that we ought to abide by the judgment of God, to whom its secrets lie naked and opened; the Lord beheld in Zacharias something worse than his words will bear. It is the same discrimination, he says, by which God distinguishes Sarah's laugh from Abraham's, though the one apparently does not differ from the other.

What the something worse was Calvin then names. Stopping at the ordinary course of nature, Zacharias ascribed less than he ought to the power of God; and they take a narrow view of his works who believe he will do no more than nature holds out as probable, as if his hand were confined to earthly means, whereas it belongs to faith to believe that more can be done than carnal reason admits. Yet Calvin will not make the failure total. There is a general faith which embraces the promise of eternal salvation, and beside it many special promises with a special faith answering to each; so a man who trusts God for the pardon of his sins may still be too much alarmed by the dread of death, too solicitous about daily food, or too anxious about his plans. Such was the unbelief here, holding the root while hesitating on the single point whether God would give him a son — and the branches of faith may be agitated by various tempests without its giving way at the root. Wesley draws the comparison that the chapter itself invites, that Zacharias disbelieved the fact while Mary had no doubt of the thing and inquired only about the manner. Clarke leaves the sternest verdict: no natural impediment has any power once God has declared his purpose, and it is impious, when we are convinced that a word is his, to demand a pledge for its fulfilment.
19:
The angel answers by giving his name, and Ellicott notes how late such names are: none appear in the Old Testament until after the Babylonian exile, and then Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael together. Since Gabriel had appeared in the very prophecies which more than any others were the germ of the Messianic expectations the people cherished, there was a fitness in his being sent now to prepare the way. Gill reports the Jewish account that the names of angels came up out of Babylon by means of the Israelites, and that it was there Daniel became acquainted with both Gabriel and Michael; he raises in passing the question of what language was spoken, and judges that since Syriac was generally understood among the Jews at the time, it is highly reasonable the angel used it. Clarke finds the name itself suited to the occasion, being compounded of the words for might and for God, and so pointing to the all-prevailing power by which the strong God could accomplish every purpose and subdue all things to himself. Barnes renders it more simply as man of God, and recalls that this was the angel deputed to tell Daniel his prayers were heard.

The second half of the self-description is where the rebuke lies. Robertson says the whole sentence is a rebuke to the doubt of Zacharias, and Wesley hears a deliberate gradation in it, enhancing the guilt step by step — I am Gabriel, a holy angel; yea, one of the highest order; not only so, but now peculiarly sent from God; and that with a message to you in particular; nay, and to show you glad tidings, such as ought to be received with the greatest readiness. Calvin turns the point outward: what had been questioned was not the messenger's veracity but the veracity of God who sent him, so that the author of the promise was treated with indignity in the person of his ambassador. He adds that the name is given for our sakes rather than the angel's, to instruct us that we must not ascribe to angels anything of their own, since whatever excellence they possess is from God — and that if the word spoken by angels was steadfast, the gospel published by the Lord of angels binds us the more.

The sign asked for is granted, and Ellicott catches the irony exactly: the demand had implied a want of faith, and so the sign took the form of a penalty. Barnes calls it both at once, a sign that the angel had come from God and that the thing would be fulfilled, and a judgment for not crediting it — there being no sin, he says, more aggravated in the sight of God than unbelief. Clarke observes that the silence was not the ordinary dumbness that proceeds from some weakness in the organs of speech, since there was no such weakness here; silence was imposed, and he should not be able to break it until the power that silenced him gave leave. Let those who are intemperate with their tongues, Clarke adds, behold both the severity and the mercy of the Lord in nine months' silence for one intemperate speech. Calvin thinks the punishment peculiarly fitted to the fault, since a man who had interrupted the promise with murmurs ought to have heard it in silence: faith has its silence, to lend an ear to the Word of God, and afterwards its turn to speak and answer Amen. Yet he finds the sentence mitigated in two ways, by its limited term and by the promise not being withdrawn — with the same gentleness, he says, God treats us daily, since when our faith is weak and we throw out many obstacles, his truth in continuing to flow toward us must break through them with a kind of violence.
21:
The delay is measured against a known custom. Barnes reports that a priest was not accustomed to remain in the temple more than about half an hour, so that when this one stayed longer the people grew apprehensive for his safety and wondered what had happened; Robertson cites the Talmud to the same effect, that the priest remained only a brief time in the sanctuary, and notes that the verb for waiting is an old word denoting mental direction, whether of hope or of fear. Clarke fills in what the half hour held — a profound silence, the people standing without engaged in mental prayer, with an allusion to the same scene in the Revelation — and observes that Zacharias had spent not only the time the incense required but whatever the discourse with the angel took up besides. Gill offers three guesses at the excess: a longer conversation than Luke reports, or amazement at the sight that kept him musing, or time given to mental prayer and confession and thanksgiving. What the crowd was waiting for, Wesley says simply, was to be dismissed with the blessing.

Calvin's interest is that the delay made the people witnesses. Zacharias had tarried beyond the usual time, which of itself suggests something uncommon; when he came out he made known by looks and gestures that he had been struck dumb, and there is reason to think there were traces of alarm in his countenance as well. From these obvious symptoms they concluded that God had appeared to him, and Calvin thinks the inference sound: it was no common accident but rather an astonishing work of God that a man should become suddenly dumb without disease and emerge from the temple, after a more than ordinary delay, in a state of amazement. He grants that there were few or no visions in that age, but the people remembered that in the time of their fathers such things had been frequent. He notes too what the crowd had been standing there to receive, since the priests, on finishing their sacred functions, were accustomed to come out into the court and bless the people from the steps.

What they perceived is stated with some care. Ellicott points out that the word is chosen as distinguished from a dream, to imply that what had been witnessed was seen with the waking sense, and that the look of awe, the strange gestures and the unwonted silence together showed the man had come under the influence of some supernatural power; the tense of the verb for beckoning, he adds, implies continued and repeated action. Robertson says the same of the gesturing, that he nodded and beckoned back and forth, and finds the decisive evidence in what was missing: they knew clearly because he could not pronounce the benediction. Barnes glosses the noun as sight or appearance, commonly applied to spirits or beings from another world, and notes that since Zacharias was unable to speak the people had no way of learning anything except by such a sign. Clarke explains why they had seen nothing themselves — the sanctuary was divided from the court by a great veil — so that they understood what had happened only from the man's own signs, signs being the one means by which a dumb man can convey his ideas to others.
23:
That he finished the week at all is what strikes the bench. Clarke observes that had Zacharias not loved the service, the loss of his speech would have made an excellent pretext for leaving at once; but since dumbness did not disable him from the sacerdotal function he saw himself bound to stay till his ministry ended, and he did not even hurry home with news his wife was so nearly concerned in. From which Clarke turns on his own profession: preachers who abandon the vineyard for some trifling bodily disorder show either that they never had a proper concern for their Master's honour or that they have lost his spirit. Barnes says the same more temperately: the occurrence and his own calamity might well have sent him home, but his duty was in the temple, and ministers are to remain at their work until genuinely unfitted for it, so that he who forsakes his post for trifling causes is unfaithful to his Master. Ellicott notes that the word for the ministration carries the idea of liturgical service, the days running from sabbath to sabbath; Robertson traces it to our liturgy, an ordinary Greek term for work done for the people.

Calvin uses the going home to explain the staying away. So long as the priests were attending in their courses they did not enter their own houses, galleries having been built round the temple walls where they had chambers; the law did not forbid a priest his house, but since those who ate the shewbread might not come near their wives, this was probably found a remedy, that being removed from temptation they might keep clear of every defilement. And they were discharged not only from their wives but from wine and strong drink. On that second half Calvin turns the argument against the law of celibacy: those who plead this precedent for perpetual continence should say why they do not also abstain from wine, since we may not separate commandments God has joined, and intercourse with wives is not so expressly forbidden as drinking is. The real solution lies in the distinction between law and gospel: a priest then stood before God to expiate the people's sins, a figure of the true Mediator, and needed something peculiar to mark him off — the design of the holy garments and the anointing — whereas the pastors Christ appointed have nothing of the kind, and may rest in the decision of the Spirit that marriage is honourable in all.

Why Elisabeth then hid herself is less obvious. Calvin rejects the suggestion that she doubted and feared ridicule if disappointed, since her own words affirm the favour as ascertained, and offers two other reasons: that until the work was manifest she might hesitate to expose it to the diversified opinions of men, the world being given to irreverent talk about God's works, and that when she was discovered all at once to be with child men would be the more moved to praise him. Wesley thinks she retired for leisure to bless God; Gill notes that she knew the story already, her husband having informed her by writing. Robertson cites Hobart's remark that Luke has almost as many words for pregnancy and barrenness as Hippocrates. On the reproach Ellicott says the words express the Jewish feeling about maternity in almost its strongest form, childlessness being more than a misfortune and seeming to imply some secret sin God was punishing — witness Rachel's cry and Hannah's bitterness of soul. Chrysostom hears only the reversal: the unfruitful rock has produced the green blade, and her joy is twofold, the mark of barrenness taken away and an illustrious offspring given — for in other births there is the coming together of parents, while this birth was the effect of heavenly grace.
26:
Gill reads the interval as a measure of rank: six months separated the two conceptions and the two births, and the same distance seems to have held between the ministries — John going before Christ as man, being his forerunner, while Christ was preferred before him as mediator and existed before him as the eternal Son of God. Ellicott notes that the reckoning runs from the period named two verses earlier, and Wesley that it dates from Elisabeth's conceiving. Calvin finds in the arrangement something far removed from the ordinary judgment of men — that God should make the beginning of the herald's generation more illustrious than that of his own Son. The prophecy about John was published in the temple and universally known, whereas Christ is promised to a virgin in an obscure town and the promise stays buried in the breast of a young woman. But it was proper that from his birth the saying should hold, that it pleased God by foolishness to save them that believe; and we should not be ashamed, Calvin adds, to take instruction from her who carried in her womb the eternal wisdom of God.

Ellicott describes the town at length: a valley among hills that rise some five hundred feet on the north of the Plain of Esdraelon, richly cultivated, the slopes clothed in spring with flowers, one side broken by a steep ridge that forms something like a precipice. From the hill behind it there is one of the finest views in Palestine; the name he derives from the Hebrew word for a branch. Clarke raises the question the address invites — since Joseph and Mary were both of David's family, whose estate lay in Bethlehem, why was the household not there? — and answers that they probably withdrew to Galilee for fear of Herod's jealousy, who had usurped a throne to which they had an indisputable right. Henry finds providence in the obscurity: a remote corner, in no reputation for religion or learning, bordering on the heathen and so called Galilee of the Gentiles, so that Christ's having his relations there intimates favour in reserve for the Gentile world — no disadvantage of place, he says, shall prejudice those for whom God has favours in store. Barnes marks the month and the town without comment; Robertson, that Gabriel is God's messenger to Mary as to Zacharias.

That she was at once a virgin and espoused is the point every voice presses. Henry takes the name as Miriam's, signifying exalted, and the lineage as royal though poor, since she went under the title of the house of David; the virginity was necessary because he was not to be born by ordinary generation, the betrothal because honour was to be put on the married state. Calvin reads the marriage as a veil held before the eyes of the world, so that one commonly supposed the son of Joseph might at length be acknowledged as the Son of God — though he rejects Origen's notion that the purpose was to hide the coming salvation from Satan. He observes that the participle means she had been engaged but not yet given as a wife, Jewish parents being accustomed to keep their daughters some time at home after betrothal. Cyril uses the same fact against two errors at once, refusing both those who teach that Christ's coming was a phantom and those who say his birth was of husband and wife: Mary is called Joseph's wife because betrothed to him, as Rachel was called Jacob's wife before the wedded state, merely because there was a promise. Chrysostom explains the timing — the angel comes before the conception rather than after, lest she be too much troubled, and stands by her in visible shape rather than in a dream, since tidings so great needed an extraordinary manifestation before the event.
27:
Ellicott is careful to say how little is known. Of Mary's parentage the canonical Gospels tell us nothing, and the apocryphal legends — her mother's name, her childhood in the Temple, the suitors whose rods were laid before the Holy Place — have left their impress on Christian art without any claim to the character even of tradition. The scanty notices are that she was a kinswoman of Elisabeth, and so possibly of the daughters of Aaron, and that she had a sister; the silence about her parents suggests an orphan, and the narrative presupposes poverty. Of Joseph he says that a village carpenter, probably older than his betrothed, must still have known himself heir of the house of David. Robertson adds the legal weight of the betrothal, which usually lasted a year and under which unfaithfulness in the bride was punished with death; Wesley, that the contract was made before witnesses some time in advance, and that God ordered the birth to fall to one espoused so that the child might have a reputed father. Clarke borrows Quesnel's contrast: the angel is sent not to the palaces of the great but to a poor maid, since the Son of God comes to humble the proud and honour poverty.

Gill puts the scene plainly, that the angel came into her house and into the room where she was; Clarke refuses to dissolve it into a dream, since divine visions are announced as such in the sacred writings, and we cannot safely attribute anything to a vision where the text does not say so. Barnes takes the greeting as equivalent to peace be with thee, and measures the honour by what it displaced — to be reckoned among the Messiah's ancestors was accounted honour enough for Abraham and David, and now the individual was designated, a poor virgin of Nazareth. He observes that the verb is absent from the next clause in the Greek, so that it may as well be read as the angel's prayer, the Lord be with thee.

The disputed word is the second one, and it divides the bench from the Vulgate rather than from each other. Ellicott says the verb is the same elsewhere translated hath made us accepted, and that the rendering full of grace has no warrant in the meaning of the word; he notes too that the closing clause is omitted in many of the best manuscripts. Robertson glosses the perfect passive as endowed with grace, and reports that the oldest manuscripts carry the blessing not here but later in the chapter. Calvin explains why grace should head the message at all: our capacities admit too slender a portion of knowledge to comprehend the greatness of God's works, so the angel first prepares the heart by meditation on undeserved favour and then enlarges it to receive an incomprehensible mystery, a conviction of the Divine goodness being the entrance of faith. From which he draws his conclusion: if Mary's happiness and righteousness flow from the undeserved love of God, and her excellence is nothing more than the Divine kindness, it is the height of absurdity to seek from her what she derives from the same quarter as ourselves — the words being a simple congratulation, which those who have turned them into a prayer both misuse and address to a person who is absent. Clarke states the limit as sharply — highly favoured as chosen before all women to be the mother of the Messiah, not the mother of God, which he calls blasphemy — and Wesley works through the parallels, that what is said here of favour was said of Noah and Moses and David, that the Lord is with thee was said to Gideon, and that Jael was called blessed above women.
29:
Ellicott notes that the word for her trouble is the one used of Zacharias, so that with her as with him the first feeling was natural terror: who was the visitor, and what did the strange greeting mean? Barnes accounts for it by accumulation — so unexpected, so sudden, so extraordinary, and so high an honour that she was filled with anxious thoughts and did not know what to make of it. Clarke says the glorious appearance left her puzzled to find the purport of the speech. Calvin observes that Luke ascribes the trouble to the words rather than the presence, and asks why the presence should be mentioned at all: perceiving something of heavenly glory in the visitor, she was seized with dread arising out of reverence for God. But Luke does not say she lost her recollection; on the contrary he records a mark of an attentive and composed mind, since she considered what the salutation meant, it having occurred to her at once that an angel is not sent for a trifling purpose. Robertson finds both states in the tenses: she was upset, and then reckoned up the reasons.

Calvin makes the fear general before he removes it. Whenever the feeblest ray of the Divine glory bursts upon us we cannot avoid alarm, since we cannot apprehend the presence of God apart from its effects; and as we are all amenable to his tribunal, fear gives rise to trembling until he manifests himself as a Father. The virgin saw in her own nation such a mass of crimes that she had reason to dread heavier punishments, so the angel removes the fear by certifying a blessing. Calvin notes the Hebrew idiom besides, that a person finds favour not when he has sought it but when it is freely offered him. Chrysostom draws the moral from the other end — he who has favour in God's sight has nothing to fear, and how shall anyone find it except by humility, since God gives grace to the humble. Ellicott prefers to keep the rendering favour here rather than grace, the latter word being fit enough but now bound up with the technicalities of theology; Robertson traces the noun to the root of the verb to rejoice, its senses beginning in sweetness and delight and carrying the notion of kindness, especially of God toward men. Barnes hears in the opening words the reassurance that the messenger brings good tidings.

Gill marks the interjection that opens the promise, a conception in a pure virgin being matter for a behold; the Persic and the Vulgate, he notes, differ over whether she saw the angel or heard him. Ellicott observes that Luke makes no reference to Isaiah's prophecy, though Mary's answer shows she understood the angel in the sense Matthew gives the prophet's words; what perplexed her was that conception and birth should be spoken of in a prediction which said nothing of her approaching marriage. Calvin thinks the angel deliberately adapted his words to Isaiah and other passages esteemed among the godly, so that the agreement between ancient prophecy and present message was pointed out on purpose. He finds the one word conceive enough to set aside the dream of Marcion and Manichaeus, since Mary brought forth no ethereal body or phantom but the fruit she had carried; and the name was given by the command of God, that our faith might be founded in heaven and not in earth. Chrysostom answers those who find it unworthy that God should inhabit a body by pointing at the sun, whose heat is felt by every body that receives its rays without its own purity being sullied — much more does the Sun of Righteousness, taking a pure body from the Virgin's womb, escape defilement and show forth his mother in greater holiness.
32:
Gill divides the greatness by office. Great in his person as God-man; great in the prophetic office, as that prophet Moses spoke of, mighty in word and deed; great as high priest, both in the oblation of himself and in his prevailing intercession; great as king; and great in his works, the miracles that proved his Deity, the redemption, and the raising of all men at the last day. Clarke reaches four heads of his own: that the human nature born of the virgin was to be united with the divine; that it should be called in a peculiar sense the Son of the most high God, since God would produce it in her womb without the intervention of man; that he should be everlasting Head of his Church; and that his kingdom should be eternal, his being the only dominion that shall never have an end. Barnes keeps to the plain sense: great in power, in wisdom, in dominion on earth and in heaven.

How much the second title proves is less agreed. Robertson notes there is no article in the Greek, and since sons of the Most High is used elsewhere of men we cannot insist on deity here, though it remains possible; Ellicott adds that the same title is afterwards heard on the lips of the demoniacs. Calvin presses the other way. The angel had said something similar of John without making him equal to Christ: the Baptist is great in his own class, while the greatness of Christ is at once explained as raising him above all creatures, since to him alone belongs the prerogative of being called God's Son. Angels and kings are so dignified in Scripture, but in common and on account of their rank, whereas God distinguishes his own Son by addressing him particularly; we are sons by adoption obtained through faith, he the only-begotten. Calvin uses this against Servetus, who argued from the future tense that Christ began to be the Son of God only when he took our flesh: the words mean that he who had been the Son from eternity would be manifested as such in the flesh, there being a wide difference between beginning to be what one was not and being made known as what one already was. Wesley says only that the title belongs to him in a more eminent sense than any man or angel can claim.

The throne raises a question of descent. Ellicott says the words at first suggest that the Virgin was herself of the house of David and the title came through her,; on the other hand both genealogies appear to give the lineage of Joseph only, so that on that view our Lord was thought of as inheriting from him despite the supernatural birth. He adds that the promise, which might well have raised the expectation of a revived kingdom of Israel, is among the most memorable instances of a prophecy fulfilled in quite another fashion than its first hearers could have imagined — and that the Evangelist took it as fulfilled in the spiritual sovereignty of the Christ is shown by his recording it in the Gospel that tells of the Crucifixion and the Ascension. Cyril meets the objection directly: if any denies the promise because Christ never sat on David's wooden throne, let him remember that the scribes sit in Moses' seat, which signifies not a wooden seat but the authority of his teaching — so seek for David's throne not the timber but the kingdom itself. The discourse is plainly of Christ and not of Solomon, whose throne did not endure as the sun. Calvin observes that the prophets always direct the hope of believers to the kingdom of David, so that it became a Jewish maxim that the safety of the church hung on that kingdom's prosperity.
33:
Gill refuses a literal reading of the house named: not the posterity of Jacob merely, but the whole Israel of God consisting of Jews and Gentiles, since as David reigned over Idumeans and Syrians as well as over Judah, so this son of his shall reign over both. Clarke takes it of all who belong to the twelve tribes; Wesley says in which all true believers are included. Barnes reads the phrase as equivalent to saying he would reign over his own church and people for ever, which he does by giving them laws, by defending them and by guiding them, and will do for ever in the kingdom of his glory. He presses the last clause: his is the only kingdom that shall never have an end, and he the only King that shall never lay aside diadem and robes, and never die.

The perpetuity nevertheless raises a difficulty, and Ellicott states both halves of it. The apparent promise is of a kingdom restored to Israel, such as the disciples still expected after the Resurrection, and it needed interpreting by events before men could see it fulfilled in the history of Christendom as the true Israel of God. Paul's language elsewhere seems at first to fix a term to the kingdom of the Christ, though closer study shows he speaks of it as a contest with the hostile forces of evil: that sovereignty may cease when the conflict is over, but it ceases by being perfected, not by passing away after the fashion of earthly kingdoms. Robertson observes that Luke reports the perpetuity without any Pauline interpretation of a spiritual Israel, though that was the true meaning and Luke knew it. Calvin explains why the seat is named at all: the throne was erected among Israel that Christ might thence subdue the whole world, and by a new adoption God has admitted the Gentiles who were formerly strangers. He adds that the promise is intelligible only of this kingdom, since the historical one was powerful under David and Solomon alone, Rehoboam hardly retaining a tribe and a half.

Mary's question is at once compared with the priest's, and every voice acquits her but one. Gill insists she did not doubt: she required no sign as Zacharias did, is nowhere charged with unbelief, and is expressly said to have believed — her words express amazement and a wish to know the manner. Ellicott sets the questions side by side: Zacharias asked by what sign he should know the words were true, whereas Mary, told of a far greater marvel and understanding the birth to be antecedent to her marriage, accepts the words in faith and seeks only to know how they will be accomplished. Calvin alone will not let her off. She appears to confine the power of God within as narrow limits as Zacharias did, concluding what lies beyond the common order of nature to be impossible, when she ought to have risen at once by faith to a power not fettered by natural means; we need not, he says, take much trouble to acquit her. Yet he grants she does not lower God's power to the level of her senses, but is carried away by a sudden impulse of astonishment, and that her embracing the promise appears from her hesitating on one point only. He also rejects as unfounded and altogether absurd the inference that she had vowed perpetual virginity, since she would then have dealt treacherously in allowing herself to be given to a husband — and it is idle to suppose a monastic life existed among the Jews. Cyril lets the wonder stand where it fell: she who bore him wondered at it herself, and the generation was immaculate and undefiled, for where the Holy Spirit breathes all pollution is taken away.
35:
Gill notes that the angel now gives an account of the manner, with things to strengthen her faith. Calvin warns it is not designed to satisfy curiosity: it leads the virgin to contemplate the power of the Spirit and surrender herself silently to his guidance. The first verb denotes an extraordinary work in which natural means have no place; the second carries an elegant metaphor, for though God's protection is often likened to a shadow, the sense here seems peculiar — the Spirit's operation would be secret, as if an intervening cloud forbade it to be seen by men; and what God conceals ought to be viewed with seriousness and adoration. Robertson takes the same figure the other way, the verb being used of the bright cloud at the Transfiguration, and hears in it the Shekinah glory, where the cloud represents the presence and power of God. Ellicott hears another aspect of the Spirit's work, quickening the dead chaos into life. Clarke agrees the allusion is to the Spirit brooding on the waters, confirming his view that Christ's human nature was a real creation in the womb.

The word therefore, linking birth to title, opens the chapter's sharpest dispute. Barnes takes the passage to prove beyond controversy that one reason Jesus was called the Son of God is that he was begotten in a supernatural manner; the body was created by the direct power of God because a Messiah atoning for others and not himself needed a human nature free from the corruption of the fall. Clarke presses that much further. The angel does not give the appellation to the divine nature at all, but to that holy thing which was to be born of the virgin, since the divine nature could not be born and had no beginning; and he says outright that the doctrine of the eternal Sonship seems to him anti-scriptural and highly dangerous, since son implies a father and so precedency in time — the phrase eternal Son being, in his judgement, a positive self-contradiction. Ellicott holds a middle position: the words do appear to rest the title on the supernatural birth rather than the eternal pre-existence, and we may accept that the angel's message was a partial and not a complete revelation, giving a sufficient reason for the name and no more than was then required.

Calvin answers in the same terms. Those who imagine Christ became the Son of God after his human generation seize on this very particle; but the conclusion is false, for though he was manifested to be the Son of God in the flesh it does not follow that he was not the Word begotten of the Father before the ages. He who had been the Son of God in his eternal Godhead appeared also as the Son of God in human flesh, and the name, which belonged to the divine essence from the beginning, is now applied unitedly to both natures. From which Calvin draws a consequence: we may venture the more freely to call God our Father, because his only Son chose to be our brother that we might have a Father in common with him. He explains the word holy the same way: as Christ had to be a real man, to expiate our sins in our flesh, so he had to be free from every spot if he was to cleanse others, and though formed of the seed of Abraham he contracted no defilement — not merely that he might abound in personal holiness, but that he might sanctify his own people. Wesley holds both halves together: the power of the Highest was exerted by the Spirit as his own, and the title belongs to Christ not only as he is God from eternity but on this account likewise. Robertson adds that the phrase was in any case a recognised designation of the Messiah.
36:
Chrysostom admires the tact of the sign. The previous words had overcome the mind of the virgin, so the angel drops to a humbler subject and persuades her by sensible things; he did not remind her of Sarah or Rebecca or Rachel, examples of ancient times, but brought forward a recent event, to strike her mind the more forcibly. For the same reason he named the age and the natural infirmity, and spoke not at the beginning of Elisabeth's conception but after six months, when the swelling of the womb could confirm it. Calvin reasons from the same instance: if neither barrenness nor old age could prevent God from making Elisabeth a mother, Mary had no reason to confine her view within the ordinary limits of nature; and the month is named because a woman usually feels the child quicken in the fifth, so the sixth removes all doubt. She ought, he grants, to have relied on the bare word of God, but the Lord condescends to strengthen his promise with this new aid, as he cheers us daily with greater indulgence still, because our faith is weaker. Barnes says the case was mentioned to inspire confidence, being almost as improbable as her own; Clarke suspects the phrase about barrenness was a name Elisabeth went by among her neighbours, and perhaps the reproach she later spoke of.

The kinship raises a small legal difficulty. Gill explains that Elisabeth might be of Levi by her father and of Judah by her mother, intermarriage between the tribes being frequent and no offence against the intention of the law, which forbade it in order to preserve each tribe's inheritance — a danger that did not arise where Levi had no inheritance at all. He allows too that cousin may be used loosely, the Jews calling any of their own nation kinsmen. Ellicott infers that either a parent of Mary was of the house of Aaron or the mother of Elisabeth of the house of David. Wesley states it more narrowly: the law forbade only heiresses to marry outside their tribe, so that others intermarried continually, particularly the families of David and Levi. Robertson cuts the knot: the word need not mean cousin, but simply relative.

Clarke hears in the angel's closing maxim the words spoken to Sarah when the birth of Isaac was foretold, and thinks Mary could not have missed the allusion. Calvin uses the sentence to correct a habit of mind. Taken strictly it means that God will do what he has promised, since no hindrance can resist his power; and they wander widely from the truth who imagine the power of God to be something lying beyond his word, for it is idle and even dangerous to argue what God can do without taking into account what he resolves to do. What the angel does here God frequently does in Scripture — employ a general doctrine to confirm one particular promise, since promises in their general form make little impression on us. All men acknowledge in words that God is almighty, yet when he promises beyond what we can comprehend we remain in doubt, only because we ascribe to his power nothing more than our senses receive. On the answer that follows Calvin notes that the virgin stops the entrance of opposing arguments and compels herself to obey, which is the real proof of faith — to hold our minds captive so that they dare not reply to God, boldness in disputing being the mother of unbelief. Barnes reads the words as resignation and faith at once. Ellicott hears more in them: a half-consciousness that the lot she accepts may bring unknown sufferings as well as untold blessedness, so that she shrinks from the awfulness of the position and yet can say what her Son would say in his own hour, not my will but thine be done.
39:
Calvin takes the journey as evidence about the faith that preceded it: the promise did not fade away with the presence of the angel but was impressed on her mind, and the haste indicates a sincere and strong affection. He asks what her object was, and rejects two answers. It was not mere inquiry, since she already cherished by faith the Son of God conceived in her womb; nor was it, as some think, to congratulate her kinswoman. More probably it was partly to strengthen her own faith and partly to celebrate the grace of God which both of them had received — for though believers are satisfied with the bare word of God, they do not disregard any of his works that help to confirm it. Henry notices the courtesy of the arrangement: Mary was the younger and the younger with child, so if they were to meet it was fittest she should travel, not insisting on the preference her conception gave her; and she went with care and expedition, not as young people commonly go abroad to visit friends, to divert herself, but to inform herself. Gill has her setting out as soon as the angel was gone, partly to use the sign she had been given, and partly to talk with Elisabeth of what God had done for each of them and praise his name together.

Where she went is not stated, and the bench divides between conjecture and refusal. Clarke names Hebron, the city of the priests in the tribe of Judah, some forty miles south of Jerusalem and upwards of seventy from Nazareth; Wesley agrees, adding that it belonged to the house of Aaron. Barnes declines to guess — some have supposed Jerusalem and others Hebron, but all is conjecture, and the most that can be said is that it was probably a Levitical city where Zacharias lived when off duty. Ellicott finds the description too vague to identify, notes that no city of the name is known, and offers Juttah, near Maon and the Judaean Carmel and so in the hill country; he adds the reflection that the journey brought the Virgin not far from the place where she was to give birth. Robertson observes that the word Luke uses for the hill country is an old one found in the Septuagint but nowhere else in the New Testament, and allows the same guess, that Judah here may stand for Juttah.

Henry reports at length a conjecture of Lightfoot's which he plainly finds attractive: that Mary was to conceive our Saviour at Hebron itself, that she may have been given some intimation of it, and that this is why she made such haste. It suits the harmony God uses in his works, on that view, that Shiloh of the tribe of Judah should be conceived in a city of Judah and of David, as he was to be born in Bethlehem, another city belonging to both; and Hebron was where the promise was given to Isaac and circumcision instituted, where Abraham had his first land and David his first crown, and where the three patriarchal couples lay interred. Henry sees no improbability in it and adds a support of his own, that Elisabeth says there shall be a performance, as though it were not performed yet but was to be performed there. From which Henry draws the general rule that those who have a good work of grace begun in them do well to consult others in the same case and compare experiences, since as in water face answers to face, so does the heart of man to man. Calvin will say only what Luke says, that the city belonged to the tribe of Judah and stood in a hilly district, from which he infers that it lay farther from Nazareth than Jerusalem did.
40:
Gill notices whom she did not greet. Mary saluted Elisabeth and not Zacharias — either because he was not at home, or because being deaf and dumb he could neither hear nor return it, or because it was not usual for women to salute men; one woman might salute another, and it was with Elisabeth she was concerned. Ellicott supposes the words were the ordinary formula, peace be with thee, perhaps joined to some congratulation on what she had heard from the angel, and adds that, so far as human sources go, the account of a scene between two women alone must have reached Luke from the Virgin herself. Robertson finds more in the greeting: her first glance at Elisabeth showed the truth of the angel's message, and the two mothers had a bond of sympathy.

What happened next divides the bench on a delicate point. Clarke takes it as the accomplishment of the earlier promise that the child should be filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother's womb: the mother is filled, and the child within her becomes sensible of the divine influence. Calvin will not go so far. He grants that sudden joy in a pregnant woman naturally moves the child, and holds that Luke means something extraordinary here; but he refuses the intricate questions, whether the infant was aware of Christ's presence or felt an emotion of piety, since Luke does not say the feeling belonged to the child, and rather intimates that this part of the divine operation took place in the mother. The filling he understands as a sudden endowment with prophecy to an unusual degree, the gifts of the Spirit not having been wanting before, but their power now appearing more abundant. Robertson keeps the middle ground: the leaping is common enough, and it was the Spirit's filling that let Elisabeth understand what had happened. Barnes lists what the filling produced — joy, a disposition to praise God, and prophetic knowledge of the child; Wesley, that the joy of her soul so affected her body that the child was moved as if it leaped for joy.

The blessing that follows repeats the angel's words, and Ellicott hears in it the poetry of the older Scriptures, noting the contrast between the same phrase applied there to the murderess Jael and here to the mother of the Lord. Calvin raises an objection to the sentence: Elisabeth seems to put Mary and Christ on an equal footing, which would be highly improper. His answer is that the second clause assigns the reason for the first, so that Mary is called blessed on account of the blessedness of her child — with the qualification that to carry Christ in her womb was not her first blessedness, being far inferior to being born again by the Spirit to a new life, though she is justly called blessed for the honour God gave her. On the next words he praises the happy medium Elisabeth keeps. The world's native depravity is such, he says, that few escape one of two faults: some, delighted with themselves, enviously despise the gifts of God in their brethren, while others praise those gifts so superstitiously as to turn them into idols — with the result that the first rank is assigned to Mary and Christ lowered as it were to the footstool. Elisabeth praises without hiding the divine glory, ascribing everything to God; and the title she gives denotes a unity of person in the two natures. Barnes is more cautious about the word Lord, which may denote divinity or merely a superior; Ellicott thinks the contrast leaves no doubt that she used it in the highest sense, since great as her own son was to be, here was the mother of one greater. Cyril takes the scene as the Spirit's own work, remarking that he recognises not virgins only but matrons also.
45:
Gill sets the two believers of the chapter against each other and makes the comparison exact. Mary was a very young woman, told things incredible to nature and reason, and she believed without objecting or asking a sign; Zacharias was a man in years, a priest by office, and he was incredulous about something far more possible, since there had been instances before in Sarah, in Hannah, and in the wife of Manoah, whereas of a virgin's conceiving there had been none. Wesley thinks it probable that Elisabeth had her husband's unbelief in mind as she spoke.
