Robertson notes that this is the first beatitude in the New Testament, and that it answers to the last one in the Gospels, spoken to Thomas to discourage his doubt: Elisabeth wishes Mary to have full faith in what the angel promised. Barnes adds that she was blessed not only in the act of believing but because the thing believed would certainly come to pass.

What follows turns on a conjunction. Ellicott says the two renderings, for there shall be and that there shall be, are equally tenable on grammatical grounds, but that internal considerations favour the second, since the first appears to make the fulfilment of the promise depend on the Virgin's faith. Clarke prefers the same arrangement: faith is here the foundation of true happiness because it receives the fulfilment of God's promises, and since whatever God has promised he intends to perform, his own authority is reason enough to believe. Robertson leaves it open, since it makes good sense either way. Calvin takes the sense that faith gives way to the divine promises so that they may obtain their accomplishment in us, and is careful to say what that does not mean. The truth of God does not depend on the will of men, and he remains true though the whole world should try to ruin his veracity; but since unbelievers are unworthy to obtain the fruit of the promises, Scripture teaches that by faith alone they are made powerful for our salvation. God offers his benefits indiscriminately to all, and faith holds out its lap to receive them, while unbelief lets them pass by without reaching us.

Calvin adds a note on the last words, that the promise had been brought by an angel and yet proceeded from God alone, whence we may infer that God wishes his Word to be paid equal honour whether he employs the ministrations of angels or of men, exactly as if he were visibly descending from heaven. Robertson steps back to the shape of the chapter: this song of Elisabeth is as real poetry as those of Mary and Zacharias, all three spoken under the power of the Holy Spirit and standing as the first New Testament hymns; every idea in the Magnificat occurs already in the Old Testament, which shows how full Mary's mind was of God's word. Barnes draws five lessons from Elisabeth's speech — that the spirit of prophecy had not entirely ceased among the Jews, that the Holy Ghost is the source of light and comfort and joy, that everything about this birth was remarkable, that the coming of the Messiah was matter of great joy to the ancient saints, and that it was a high honour to be the mother of the world's Redeemer. He then turns sharply on an inference drawn from the last of them, that the honour warrants worship of the Virgin and prayer offered to her, which he calls an idolatry as gross as any: it is nowhere commanded in the Bible, worship of any being but God is expressly forbidden, and it is besides absurd to suppose that she could be in all places at once to hear the prayers of thousands.
46:
Ellicott introduces the song as the first of the great canticles Luke records, which since the time of Caesarius of Arles, who first brought them into public worship, have belonged to the hymnal treasures of Western Christendom. He supposes the Virgin either committed the words to writing at the time or remembered them afterwards, possibly with some natural modification, and notes that the song is manifestly built on Hannah's, both in its opening words and in much of its substance — which tells us something of the hopes and the reading of the maiden of Nazareth. Clarke marks the same descent and adds a textual curiosity, that two copies of the Itala and some books mentioned by Origen give the song to Elisabeth instead. Robertson reports that Harnack argued the same case from a few Latin manuscripts, and dismisses it: Mary is correct, and she draws her material from the Old Testament and sings in the noblest strain. Clarke also disputes the common claim that this is the first piece of poetry in the New Testament, since the angel's address to Zacharias, his address to the virgin, and Elisabeth's answer are all delivered the same way and all reduce to the hemistich form of Hebrew verse.

The verb she opens with is not to be taken literally, and every voice says so. Barnes gives its range — to make great, then to extol, to praise, to celebrate — and rules that here it means not to make great but to increase in our estimation. Clarke says the same from the lexicon, that the word signifies to celebrate with words and extol with praises, which is the only way God can be magnified at all, since nothing can be added to one who is infinite and eternal; the way to magnify him is to show forth the acts in which he has manifested his greatness. Gill puts it as ascribing greatness rather than conferring it, and notes that Mary did this not in lip and word only but with the whole soul, and that she speaks throughout in the prophetic style, of things as already done which were then doing or shortly to be done. Wesley adds that she spoke under a prophetic impulse, and said several things which perhaps she did not herself then fully understand.

Whether soul and spirit are two things is a smaller question. Robertson will not press the difference: Bruce calls them synonyms in parallel clauses, Vincent makes the soul the principle of individuality and the spirit the point of contact between God and man, but it is doubtful whether the threefold division of man is to be insisted on at all. He does mark the tone, that Mary is not excited as Elisabeth was, but breathes a spirit of composed rapture. Calvin takes them for two faculties, the one the understanding and the other the seat of the affections, and observes that what stands second here comes first in order, since the will is not set going to praise God unless a rejoicing of spirit goes before it — sadness and anxiety lock up the soul and restrain the tongue from celebrating the goodness of God. He notes too why the title Saviour belongs just here: until God has been recognised as a Father the mind is not free for true and full joy, and the Greek word means not that he once delivered but that he is the author of an eternal salvation. Ellicott thinks the name was chosen for its meaning, which was the very work she had been told would be her Son's. Wesley draws the sharpest consequence: she rejoiced in the hope of salvation through faith in him, which is a blessing common to all believers, more than in being his mother after the flesh, which was an honour peculiar to herself.
48:
What the low estate means is disputed, and the two oldest voices here pull in opposite directions. Augustine reads it as the virtue: O true lowliness, he exclaims, which has borne God to men, given life to mortals and opened the gates of Paradise — the lowliness of Mary was made the heavenly ladder by which God descended upon earth. He glosses regarded as approved, since many seem lowly whose lowliness God does not regard, for if they were truly lowly their spirit would rejoice not in the world but in God. Calvin denies flatly that the word means any quality of mind at all. It does not denote submission or modesty, as he says ignorant men have foolishly imagined, but a mean and despicable condition, so that the sense is: I was unknown and despised, and that did not prevent God from deigning to cast his eyes upon me. This, he adds, was no cry of pretended humility but the honest statement of a conviction engraven on her mind, since she was of no account in the eyes of the world and her estimate of herself was nothing more. Robertson keeps the literal sense too — the bride of a carpenter, and yet to be the mother of the Messiah. Gill offers both readings: the outward one, that David's family was so reduced that its seat had moved from Jerusalem to Nazareth, and the spiritual one, of the estate into which the fall has brought all mankind.

Barnes draws the general rule out of the particular case. Notwithstanding her humble rank and poverty God showed her favour, which teaches what the Bible teaches elsewhere at length, that he is no respecter of persons and is not influenced by wealth or honour or office, but seeks the humble and gives his richest blessings to those who feel they need them. Clarke says the same of the verb: God visited her in her humiliation in the most compassionate manner, drawing the reasons of his conduct not from any excellence in her but from his own eternal kindness. Ellicott notices that the noun is the same word she had used of herself when she first consented, and marks it as the character she was now ready to accept, whatever it might involve.

The last clause has had a long history, and the bench is uneasy about it. Ellicott grants that the words have been partly instrumental in bringing about their own fulfilment, but asks what a vision of the future they must have implied on the part of a village maiden — that not her kinswoman only but all generations should join in that beatitude. Robertson notes that Elisabeth had already pronounced one such beatitude, and that another follows later in the Gospel, but insists this is a very different thing from the worship of Mary. Barnes agrees it is right to consider her highly favoured and happy, and denies that this warrants worshipping her or praying to her: Abraham was blessed in being the father of the faithful, Paul in being the apostle to the Gentiles, Peter in first preaching the gospel to them, and who would think of praying to Abraham or Paul or Peter? Clarke puts it as an injury to Mary herself, since this was the character by which alone she wished to be known, and those who address her as Queen of Heaven give her names he thinks her pure soul would abhor, which belong properly to God her Saviour. Calvin argues from the structure of her own sentence: she makes her happiness consist in nothing whatever but what she acknowledges to have been bestowed on her, and mentions nothing but the work of God — so that nothing could be more disrespectful to her than to rob the Son of God of what is his own in order to clothe her with the plunder.
49:
Augustine answers the question the clause invites by piling up paradoxes: what great things has he done for you, but that a creature, you gave birth to the Creator, a servant, you brought forth the Lord, and that through you God redeemed the world and restored it to life? Gill names the same thing more soberly as a new and unheard-of work, that a virgin should conceive and bear a Son who is himself the mighty God — which is why she describes the author of it as he that is mighty. Clarke draws the movement of the whole verse: as God fills her with his goodness she empties herself to him in praises, and sinking into her own nothingness confesses that God alone is all in all.

On the last three words the bench divides in an instructive way. Barnes takes holy in its strict sense and makes it the highest honour she can render: God is free from sin, injustice and impurity; the name is often put for God himself, the proper name being Jehovah, a word expressive of his essential being, which is why a common or profane use of it is solemnly forbidden. Clarke suspects the Greek is translating something else, and that the word Mary actually used was one we sometimes render holy but whose proper meaning is abundant goodness, exuberant kindness — a sense that agrees far better, he thinks, with the clause about mercy that immediately follows. Calvin keeps to reverence rather than either purity or kindness: the name of God is called holy because it is entitled to the highest reverence, and whenever it is mentioned it ought at once to remind us of his adorable majesty. He marks a structural break here too, since with these words Mary leaves the grace shown in her own person and begins to celebrate the power and judgements and mercy of God in general.

The mercy that follows is bounded by a condition, and how tightly is disputed. Calvin takes the clause from the solemn form of the covenant, in which God promises to be the God of Abraham's seed after him in their generations, and reads it as the favour God continues to show his own people after their death, loving their children and their children's children. But since not all who descend from Abraham after the flesh are the true children of Abraham, Mary confines the promise to those who truly worship God — which leaves no support for the vain confidence of hypocrites who boast of God as their Father while being the spurious children of the saints. A universal covenant was made with that posterity, he grants, but as stones moistened by rain do not grow soft, the promised righteousness is kept from unbelievers by their own hardness of heart. To the objection that this makes godliness earn the grace it receives, he answers that the fear itself is part of the mercy, God bestowing reverence for his majesty on the children of the godly rather than looking idly down from heaven to see who deserves it. Barnes defines the fear by contrast: not what a servant feels toward a cruel master, or a man toward a precipice or the plague, but what a dutiful child feels toward a kind and virtuous father, a fear of injuring his feelings or dishonouring him by our life. Robertson confirms that the word here carries its reverential sense, the meaning of dread belonging to other passages. Ellicott hears the clause opening outward instead: as read by those for whom Luke wrote, the words would almost seem to foreshadow the gospel of the Apostle of the Gentiles, since men who feared God were to be found not only among the children of Abraham but in every nation.
51:
Clarke reports a graded vocabulary Grotius had observed: God's efficacy is represented by his finger, his great power by his hand, his omnipotence by his arm — the plague of lice being the finger of God, the plagues in general his hand, and the destruction of Pharaoh's host his arm. Calvin reads the same word as a contrast with every other aid, so that Mary means God rested satisfied with his own power, employed no companions in the work, and called none to help him. Robertson renders it made might, a Hebrew conception, and notes six aorists in this one sentence, none answering to our English idiom. Wesley observes that she speaks prophetically of things as done which God was only about to do. Barnes marks the widening of the song here: the words have no particular reference to God's mercy toward Mary, since from his goodness to herself she enlarges to his goodness at large — which is the nature of true piety, for it does not terminate in God's mercy toward ourselves.

Who the proud are is left open, and Ellicott lists the candidates without choosing: the potentates of the world she lived in, Herod and the Emperor of Rome; the men of Jerusalem who despised Galilee; those of the other Galilean towns who despised Nazareth; or, less probably, those of Nazareth itself who despised the carpenter and his betrothed. Clarke takes the verb as scattering abroad, as a whirlwind scatters dust and chaff, and derives the adjective from the words meaning above and I show — men who wish to be noticed before all others and feel a sovereign contempt for everyone else; while they lay their plans and imagine success waiting at their right hand, the whirlwind of God's displeasure blows and they and their machinations are dissipated together. Calvin finds the same figure in the verb, from the putting to flight of a defeated enemy, and dwells on the phrase about the imagination of their hearts: their pride being outrageous and their covetousness insatiable, they pile their deliberations into an immense heap and build the tower of Babel, until God, having looked down a while in silent mockery on their splendid preparations, scatters the whole mass, as a building is overturned and its parts flung wide.

Ellicott traces the next noun to the word that gives us dynasty, used elsewhere of the eunuch of great authority under Candace and once as a divine title, and here of human rulers generally. Barnes suspects a particular case behind the general one, since Mary was celebrating God's mercies to her own family and it was natural to recall how Saul was overcome and David taken from the sheepfold to the throne. From that he draws a rule: men are often raised by industry and talent and the favour of God from humble stations to places of great trust, and those so elevated, if they have right feelings, will not despise their former companions — no conduct being more odious than to be ashamed of our birth or of the humble circumstances of our friends. Gill offers three readings at once: kings put down in the ordinary course of providence, the mighty angels cast from their seats of bliss for opposing the incarnation, and the monarchies of this world broken by the kingdom of the Messiah, at first as mean as a stone cut out of a mountain. Calvin uses the verse against a rival account of such reversals: Mary ascribes to the providence and judgements of God what ungodly men call the game of Fortune. Yet he denies this makes God despotic, tossing men up and down like balls: it is a just government founded on the best reasons, though they escape our notice, and if princes brought a sceptre from the womb and thrones never fell, all acknowledgement of God's providence would disappear.
53:
Clarke pictures God daily feeding multitudes at his gates, poor and rich alike dependent on him: the poor man comes through a sense of want and is fed, the rich man through the lust of gain, to get more added to his abundance, and is sent away empty — not merely given nothing more, but often deprived of what he had. Barnes says the same: the poor come that their daily wants may be supplied, the rich with lofty hearts and insatiable desires that their riches may be increased — better to be poor and go to God for daily bread than rich and forget our dependence on him. Ellicott hears the beatitudes of the Sermon on the Plain anticipated here, with both a literal and a spiritual fulfilment: those who trusted in earthly riches and those who gloried in a fancied spiritual wealth were alike sent empty away, while the hungry who craved a higher blessedness were filled. Gill names the hungry as those who longed for the Messiah's coming — Simeon, Anna, and all who looked for redemption in Israel.

The verb rendered holpen is the pivot of the next verse. Robertson defines it as laying hold of a thing with a view to help or succour, and notes that the noun beside it means servant here rather than son or child, its usual sense. Barnes makes the image more precise, of taking hold of one to help him up when he is in danger of falling. Calvin calls it an elegant metaphor of taking a falling person by the hand, and insists the state of the nation warranted it: the public instruction retained almost nothing pure, the government of the Church was in the greatest confusion and breathed nothing but shocking barbarity, the order of civil society no longer subsisted, and the people were torn like wild beasts by the Romans and by Herod — so that the restoration was the more glorious for being one which so desperate a case gave no ground to expect. Clarke narrows the falling to a single house: the family of David was ready to fall and rise no more, and Jesus, born of the last branch of the regal line, revived it and restored the dominion.

Who is meant by Israel is the usual question. Gill answers that it is not the natural posterity of Jacob but the elect among them, since all were not Israel who were of Israel, and not those only but the chosen among the Gentiles, who together make up the whole Israel of God. Ellicott hears the hymn turn outward at this point: up to here it has been personal thanksgiving, and now the whole soul of the maiden of Nazareth is with her people, her joy in the great things done for her resting on their being great things for Israel too. He adds a note on the date: a hope of restoration voiced as already realised suggests an early hymn, since by the time Luke wrote it was the rejection of Israel that occupied men's minds. Calvin explains the last clause as the reason for the whole: God lifted up the fallen nation to give an illustration of his mercy, and Mary says he remembered that mercy because he might have seemed in some sort to have forgotten it while he allowed his people to be so fearfully afflicted. Since the human mind forms no conception of the divine mercy except as it is declared in the word, she directs her attention and ours to the promises — which is why Calvin infers that she was unusually well acquainted with Scripture, the expectation of a Messiah being general in that age while few had so pure a knowledge. Clarke takes the mercy to be the covenant made with Abraham, in which salvation was promised to all the nations of the earth.
55:
The English hides a difficulty in the construction, and Ellicott sets it out. As the sentence stands in our version the words about Abraham and his seed look like an apposition explaining our forefathers; in the Greek they stand in a different connection and belong to what went before, so that the sense runs, to remember his mercy — as he spake to our forefathers — to Abraham and to his seed for ever. The mercy shown to Abraham, on that reading, was working still. Calvin agrees that the clause about the fathers is to be read as a parenthesis, but denies that the connection is as close as some make it: Mary is not merely identifying the fathers to whom God spoke, but extending the power and the result of the promises to all Abraham's posterity, so long as they are his true seed.

That qualification does the work. Calvin observes that the covenant in view here was made in a peculiar manner with Abraham and his descendants, whereas the promises given earlier to Adam and to Noah looked indiscriminately to all nations; and since many of Abraham's children after the flesh have been cut off by unbelief and thrown out as degenerate from his family, we who were strangers are admitted by faith and reckoned his true seed. Wesley says it in four words, that the seed meant is the spiritual seed, all true believers. Barnes takes the promise particularly referred to as the one now about to be fulfilled concerning the Messiah, while allowing that all the other mercies conferred on the children of Israel are included with it; he also reads the closing words for ever back into the previous verse. Gill traces the speaking to three fathers in turn — to David, of whose family Mary was, to Jacob, of whose stock she was, and to Isaac, in whom the seed was to be called.

The length of the visit is fixed with some care. Gill notes that three months was the term the Jewish doctors laid down for determining whether a woman was with child, as in cases of divorce or death, and that by the end of it Mary had full satisfaction about the sign the angel had given her, and must have been fully assured of her own condition besides. Clarke observes that on some reckonings the departure came only a few days before the birth of John, since nine months had by then elapsed since Elisabeth conceived. Ellicott feels the pull of both possibilities: the time is brought so close to the birth that we might well think the Virgin waited for it, and yet the next verse seems almost to imply that she had already gone — in any case we may think of those months as a time of much communion of heart and hope over the great things God had done and was about to do for Israel. Calvin thinks she had no other reason for staying so long than to enjoy that exhibition of divine grace which the angel had named for the confirming of her faith. He adds what the whole narrative is for: the birth of John was distinguished by various miracles which gave reason to expect something great in the child, since the Lord determined to confer remarkable tokens on him from the womb, that he might not afterwards come forward out of the crowd as an obscure and unknown person to discharge a prophet's office. Wesley notes only that she returned to her own house, and thence soon after to Bethlehem.
57:
Gill counts the months out: the nine were now complete, since the angel came to Mary in the sixth month of Elisabeth's pregnancy and Mary stayed about three, and he supposes she had left in order to avoid the company that would gather at the delivery. Clarke reports the alternative reckoning, that the three months of the visit preceded the birth and completed the term, so that the only remaining difficulty is whether Mary went to Hebron immediately after the annunciation or waited before making the journey. Henry draws a lesson from there being a term at all: though the child was conceived by miracle he continued in the womb according to the ordinary course of nature, as our Saviour did after him, so promised mercies are to be expected when the full time is come, and not before.

Gill places the company in and about Hebron, whether of the house of Aaron or of the tribe of Judah, to both of which Elisabeth was related; Henry, following Lightfoot, makes the distinction sharper, the priests of Aaron's family in the city being the kindred and the children of Judah in the fields and villages round about being the neighbours. Ellicott prefers kindred to cousins as covering a wider range of relations than our own word does, and thinks the wording implies they had heard something of the vision in the Temple and of what was foretold of the child's greatness. He notices too that the phrase for what God had done uses the verb that opens the Magnificat, so the sentence may be read as an echo of it; Robertson marks the same verb and adds that the imperfect pictures a continual joy, its prefix carrying the sense of rejoicing together. Henry finds two regards in the scene at once — a pious regard to God, since they acknowledged that the Lord had magnified his mercy, many things concurring to make it great, that she had been long barren and was now old, but especially that the child should be great in the sight of the Lord; and a friendly regard to Elisabeth, since when she rejoiced they rejoiced with her.

Clarke turns that into three obligations. It is a duty of humanity, since we are members of one another, and he who rejoices in his neighbour's prosperity increases his neighbour's happiness and gets an addition to his own. It is a duty of charity, to be performed with sincerity: in the polite world no duty is better fulfilled in word, while sincerity is utterly banished and both parties know the compliments mean nothing — and the man who does not take a sincere part in his neighbour's prosperity will soon feel ample punishment in jealousy and envy. And it is a duty of religion, since these neighbours saw that God had magnified his mercy and acknowledged his hand in the work. Calvin leaves open whether they measured the kindness simply by her having a child at all, or whether they had already heard that an angel appeared to Zacharias; on either view it was no ordinary favour that a barren woman at a very advanced age should bring forth out of the course of nature. He notes what the eighth day then made of the occasion: people assemble from a sense of duty or from courtesy, as is customary, and God takes the opportunity to make them witnesses and spectators of his power. From the size of the gathering he infers a practice: though children were circumcised at home, it was not done without collecting a numerous assembly, and with good reason, since this was a common sacrament of the church and not properly administered in a private manner.
59:
Chrysostom sets the rite in its whole history. Circumcision was first delivered to Abraham as a mark of distinction, that the patriarch's race might be preserved in unmixed purity and so be able to obtain the promises; but now that the promise of the covenant is fulfilled the sign attached to it is removed, so that through Christ circumcision ceased and baptism came in its place — though it was right that John should first be circumcised. He offers two reasons why the eighth day was appointed in mercy: because in its most tender years a child more easily bears the cutting of the flesh, and because the very operation reminds us that the thing was done for a sign, since so young a child scarcely distinguishes anything around him. Clarke draws a different consequence from the same delay: had circumcision been essential to an infant's salvation God would not have ordered it deferred to the eighth day, since in every country multitudes die before that age — and baptism, which is generally allowed to have been substituted for it, is no more necessary to an infant's salvation than circumcision was, both being signs of the covenant, and neither on that account to be neglected. Gill notes that the eighth day was the time fixed by the ordinance, though it was not always kept and circumcision was sometimes deferred, the exact day being judged most commendable. Ellicott compares the occasion to the baptism of infants among Christians, a day when relatives were invited as witnesses and which was commonly followed by a feast.

The naming belonged to the same day, and Chrysostom explains the order: after the circumcision the name was conferred, because we must first receive the seal of the Lord and then the name of man — or else because no one is worthy to have his name written in the book of life who has not first cast aside the fleshly lusts which circumcision signifies. Barnes and Clarke agree that among the Jews the name was given at the circumcision and that the eldest son ordinarily received his father's. Ellicott explains how the company came to be naming him at all: the choice commonly rested with the father, but the kinsfolk seem to have assumed that in his dumbness the duty had devolved on them, and by a custom not uncommon they showed their respect for him by choosing his name. Robertson catches the tense, which is conative — they were trying to call him so.

Calvin takes the occasion for a short history of naming. Names were originally given either from some occurrence or by prophetic inspiration, to point out some secret work of God; but after a long period, when there was such a profusion of them that it became inconvenient to form new ones every day, people contented themselves with the old received names and called their children after their ancestors — so that before the father of John there had been many a Zacharias. Use and wont, he adds drily, is generally taken for law, and that is why these people argued that the prevailing custom ought to be followed here. He will not pretend there is any sacredness in a name, and yet holds that no judicious person will deny that believers ought in this matter to make a godly and profitable selection, giving their children such names as may serve to instruct and admonish them, and so taking the names of holy fathers, for the purpose of exciting their children to imitate them, rather than adopting those of ungodly persons. Ellicott says much the same of what a name was for, that it should bear witness to the prayers of the parents and to the child's own relation to the God of his fathers.
60:
How the mother knew the name is a small puzzle with a simple answer. Barnes and Ellicott both suppose that Zacharias had told her by writing, and Ellicott adds that what follows shows the writing-tablet had been in frequent use. Calvin leaves open whether she spoke by inspiration, but thinks it likely that a man who had seen what his slowness to believe had cost him would take care to inform his wife of what the angel enjoined, since otherwise he would not have obeyed the command at all. Wesley prefers the shorter explanation, that she spoke by revelation or a particular impulse from God. Clarke finds the whole household named significantly: Zachariah is the memorial of Jehovah, Elisabeth the rest of my strong God, and John, which he would always write Jehochanan, the grace or mercy of Jehovah — a name given because the child was to go before and proclaim the God of all grace.

The objection of the relatives is a matter of custom rather than of taste. Barnes explains that the Jewish tribes and families were kept distinct, and that to avoid confusion in the genealogical tables they probably used only those names found among their ancestors, with the added motive, common to all peoples, of respect for honoured parents. Clarke gives the same account and notes that the tables were carefully preserved in each family for the sake of distinguishing inheritances, so that a name never before used in any branch of the family would naturally be resisted. Ellicott draws an inference of another kind from the absence: it probably shows that Zacharias did not belong to the circle related to the Sadducean high priests, among whom the name does appear some thirty years later. Gill checks a version against the fact, since the Persic makes them say there was no one of this name in Israel, which cannot be true, Jochanan being a very common name, though not in this family.

That they resorted to signs settles a question about the father's condition. Ellicott takes it as almost certain that Zacharias had lost hearing as well as speech and had passed into the state of one naturally a deaf mute; Robertson notes the imperfect tense, the repeated action usual in making signs. On the tablet itself the notes converge: Ellicott describes the tablets in common use throughout the Roman empire as wooden, covered with a thin coat of wax and written on with the sharp point that survives in our word style, while Robertson adds that the same word was used of a physician's note-book. Ellicott hears something emphatic in the present tense of the answer — his name is John — since this was not a question open for discussion, the name having been given already; and he thinks the general astonishment confirms the deafness, there being no ground for wonder if the father had heard the debate. Clarke reports a friend's proposal to redistribute the verses, on the ground that a man whose mouth was not opened until after the naming could not have asked for the tablet, and rejects it, since neither the words of the Greek nor their construction will bear it; he does move the clause about their marvelling forward, holding that the people wondered not at the choice of name but at the speech restored that instant. Calvin sees a design in the timing: the benefit was delayed to that day on purpose, to fix the eyes of men on the child, and Zacharias spoke not only to testify gratitude but to let his neighbours know why the punishment had fallen on him — not ashamed to unite his own dishonour with the praises of the divine glory, so that it became universally known that this birth was no accidental or ordinary event.
65:
The fear that fell on the neighbourhood is not the fear of danger. Robertson says it is not terror but religious awe at contact with the supernatural, the same word used of Zacharias in the temple, and notes that the verb for the spreading of the news is an imperfect describing continuous talk passing back and forth among the people. Barnes and Gill agree that the word denotes reverence, the remarkable circumstances of the birth and the sudden restoration of speech convincing them that God was present. Clarke locates the impression precisely: the inhabitants of Hebron and its environs, who knew the circumstances of Zacharias and Elisabeth, perceived that God had visited them in a remarkable manner, and this begot a more than ordinary reverence — so that, he adds, the salvation of one often becomes an instrument of good to the souls of many. He thinks the people of that hill country an open and honest-hearted sort, readier than townspeople to acknowledge the interposition of God. Ellicott describes the district as the mountain plateau south of Jerusalem, reaching its highest point at Hebron, and reads the verse as tracing the gradual spread of the report outward from the immediate neighbourhood.

Calvin uses the same fear to say what miracles are for. It proceeded from a feeling of the divine power, and the works of God ought to be contemplated with such reverence as to affect our minds in earnest; he does not amuse us with miracles as with a pastime, but arouses the senses of men which he sees to be stupefied and asleep. Yet many derived no lasting advantage from the impression, since when John began to exercise his office there were few who remembered what wonders had attended his birth. That is why Calvin holds the report was spread abroad not merely for the sake of those who heard it but to establish the certainty of the miracle in all ages. And he sees in the failure a general mirror of human ingratitude: while trifling and frivolous occurrences remain firmly in our minds, the things which ought to produce a constant recollection of God's favours fade at once. He is careful not to overstate it — Luke is not speaking of stupid men or open despisers, since he says they laid the words up in their hearts; some doubtless continued to remember, but the greater part rapidly shook off the fear they had felt.

The question they asked is commonly mistranslated, and Ellicott corrects it: not what kind of child this should be, but what the child would grow to. He notes that some good manuscripts supply a conjunction before the last clause, making the hand of the Lord the reason for the question, and explains the idiom — the hand standing for what we more commonly call the guidance or providence of God, one of those vivid expressions the Hebrews could use more boldly than other nations precisely because they had clearer thoughts of God as not made after the similitude of men. Barnes glosses it as aid, protection and favour, since we stretch out the hand to help those we wish to assist, and mentions that some take the words as part of the neighbours' own speech. Robertson treats the clause as Luke's own explanation added to the supernatural events, and observes that the phrase occurs only in his writings; he notes too that the people laid these things up as Mary would afterwards do. Clarke draws the inference the neighbours drew — that after so many extraordinary things God had surely designed the child for some extraordinary purpose — and says they waited patiently to see what he would work. Wesley glosses the hand as the peculiar power and blessing of God.
67:
Calvin explains what the filling adds to a man who already had the Spirit. The servants of God receive more abundantly a grace of which at other times they were not destitute, and so the Spirit is said to be given to the prophets — not that they otherwise wanted it, but that its power was more fully exerted in them when the hand of God brought them into public view for the discharge of their office. He notes how closely Luke joins the two clauses, which implies that divine inspiration rested on Zacharias in an extraordinary measure, so that he did not speak as a man or a private person but that all he uttered was heavenly instruction; Paul likewise couples prophecy with the Spirit, teaching us that to despise instruction is to quench the Spirit's light. And it was a remarkable instance of God's goodness, Calvin adds, that the man not only recovered the speech he had lacked for nine months but had his tongue made the organ of the Holy Ghost. Henry says the same of the reversal: God not only forgave the unbelief, which was signified by discharging him from its punishment, but filled him with the Spirit and put this honour on him, as a specimen of the abounding of grace toward believers. Gill notes that his wife had been so filled before him.

What prophesying means here is disputed in a small way. Clarke takes the word in what he calls its proper acceptation, of predicting or foretelling future events, since Zacharias speaks not only of what God had done but of what he was about to do in order to save a lost world. Ellicott prefers the wider sense of an inspired utterance of praise, and offers an account of the hymn's origin: it appears as the report, written probably by Zacharias himself, of the praises uttered in the first moments of his recovered speech, so that we may think of it as expressing the pent-up thoughts of the months of silence — the fire had long been kindling, and at last he spake with his tongue. Barnes resolves the difference by allowing the word all three senses at once, to foretell, to celebrate the praises of God, and to teach or preach, and observing that this song partakes of all three, being principally employed in praise while also predicting the character and preaching of John. Robertson notes that nearly every phrase in it comes from the Psalms and the Prophets, and that Zacharias, like Mary, had caught the Messianic message in its highest meaning.

Henry is struck by what the song leaves out. Nothing is said of the private concerns of his own family, of the reproach rolled away from it or the reputation put on it, though no doubt he found a time to give thanks for that with his household; here he is wholly taken up with the kingdom of the Messiah and the public blessings to be brought in by it, since he could have had little pleasure in the fruitfulness of his own vine had he not foreseen the good of Jerusalem and peace upon Israel. Henry observes too that Old Testament prophecy is often expressed in praises and new songs, and that the beginning of New Testament prophecy takes the same form; and he asks why a man speaking of a redemption for the world should call God the Lord God of Israel, answering that to Israel the prophecies and promises and types of that redemption had hitherto been given, and that Israel as a chosen people was a type of the elect out of all nations. Wesley makes the same point about proportion from the other end, that Zacharias speaks of Christ chiefly and of his own son only, as it were, incidentally.
68:
Gill begins with the form of words, a blessing probably in use ever since Israel became a body politic, and is careful about what blessing God can mean: not invoking a blessing on him, since there is none greater of whom to ask one, nor conferring one, but praising and glorifying him. Calvin asks why the God whose government the whole world is subject to should be named the God of Israel, and answers that the Redeemer had been promised to the seed of Abraham in a peculiar manner. The verb that follows carries an implied contrast, since the face of God had for a time been turned from those unhappy children, sunk so deep in calamity that no one supposed his eye was on them. Ellicott makes the same point with a date attached: the four centuries since the last of the prophets are thought of as a time when the face of the Lord was turned away, and now he looks on his people again — not to visit them for their offences, but to deliver. Barnes and Robertson trace the verb from looking upon, to looking in order to learn someone's state, to visiting in order to give aid.

What the second verb means is set out at length. Barnes renders it literally, that God has made a ransom for his people: a ransom was the price paid to deliver a captive taken in war, and the death of Jesus in the place of sinners is what God accepts instead of their eternal sufferings — not itself a punishment, since punishment supposes personal crime, but an equivalent showing the same hatred of sin. Clarke takes the word in its strict sense of ransoming a captive from the enemy by paying a price, and quotes Josephus on Herod paying three hundred talents for his brother. Ellicott observes how large an element the thought of deliverance through a ransom was in the Messianic expectation of the time, and notes that the past tense is prophetic foresight seeing the end of what had only begun — the next verse making clear that Zacharias looked for the redemption not through his own child but through the Son of Mary, as yet unborn. Calvin draws a further consequence: since those whom God redeems must be prisoners and this redemption is spiritual, even the holy fathers were freed from the yoke of sin only through the grace of Christ, and to the objection that believers who died earlier must then have been slaves all their lifetime he answers that the power and efficacy of that one redemption have been the same in all ages.

The horn is a figure with more than one possible source. Chrysostom takes it simply for power, glory and honour, drawn metaphorically from the brute creatures, to whom God has given horns for defence and for ornament. Barnes agrees the strength of horned animals lies there, but suggests the image may come instead from the Jewish altar, at each of whose corners was a projection called a horn, which a man in danger might lay hold of — so that the Redeemer is called the horn of salvation because those who flee to him are safe. Clarke prefers the same altar, adding that Christ is a new altar to which whoever flees will find refuge, and canvasses others besides: that the Chaldee paraphrast sometimes renders the word kingdom, and that a horn filled with fruits was the old emblem of abundance. Wesley reads the figure for honour, plenty and strength together, and the whole phrase as meaning a glorious and mighty Saviour. Calvin reads it as saving power: when the throne of David was cast down and the people scattered, the hope of salvation had to all appearance perished, and Zacharias alludes to those predictions which promise a sudden revival when affairs have become desperate.
70:
Calvin explains why the prophets are summoned at this point: so that the salvation brought by Christ should not be thought doubtful on the score of novelty. They were raised up at different times and yet teach with one consent that salvation is to be expected from Christ alone, and when he comes forth adorned with the testimonies of all of them our faith rests on a truly solid foundation. Zacharias calls them holy, Calvin adds, to secure greater authority for their words, since these were not inconsiderable or ordinary witnesses but of the first rank, separated from the common people by divine authority and furnished with a public commission. Barnes lists the most striking of them — Jacob, Moses, Isaiah — and enters one caution: the phrase since the world began is not to be taken literally, for there were no prophets immediately after the creation, and the expression is a general one. Wesley takes the opposite line in a sentence, that there were prophets from the very beginning; Ellicott stands between, thinking the words more than a lofty paraphrase for of old time and hearing in them a reference to the first promise in Genesis as well as to Abraham, who is the earliest man actually called a prophet. Robertson would simply render it from of old.

How the prophets are to be read Calvin then states as a rule. To inquire minutely how each one gave testimony to Christ would lead into a long dissertation; it is enough that they all uniformly make the hope of the people, that God would be gracious to them, rest entirely on that covenant which was founded on Christ. Our chief attention is therefore due to the signature of the divine covenant, and whoever neglects this will never understand anything in the prophets at all — which is why, in Calvin's judgement, the Jews wander wretchedly in reading Scripture, giving their whole study to words and missing the main design. Gill finds in the clause both the veracity of God in his promises and the earliness of the intimations he gave about the Messiah.

Who the enemies are is the one real dispute in these verses. Ellicott takes them as the men present to the speaker's own thoughts — the Roman conquerors of Judaea, with the Idumaean house of Herod perhaps among those who hate. Everyone else reads them spiritually. Clarke argues from the inspiration itself that the salvation must be spiritual, and names Satan, death and sin, of which sin is the most dangerous and properly the only enemy we have to fear, since Satan is outside us and can have no power over us except what he gets through sin, while death is only in our flesh and will be destroyed on the morning of the resurrection. Barnes lists man's sins, his carnal propensities and lusts, and the great adversary with his angels; Gill adds the world, and the law as the killing letter, and death as the last enemy to be destroyed. Calvin says Zacharias was well aware that the principal war of the church of God is not with flesh and blood but with Satan and all his armament, and though the Church is attacked by outward foes too and delivered from them by Christ, the kingdom of Christ being spiritual, the discourse relates chiefly to the prince of this world. He draws two consequences: that men out of Christ lie prostrate under the tyranny of the devil, since otherwise Christ would not be delivering his people out of his hand; and that so long as the Church continues her pilgrimage in the world she lives among her foes, and would be exposed to their violence if Christ were not always at hand to grant assistance.
72:
Ellicott finds a hidden signature in the verse. After the manner of the ancient prophets, he thinks, it plays on three names at once: performing mercy alludes to John, which means the Lord be merciful; remembering his holy covenant to Zacharias, whom Jehovah remembers; and the oath of the next verse to Elisabeth, the oath of my God — a play obvious in the Aramaic of the hymn, which survives only in its Greek version. He takes the covenant to be the one made with Abraham, and observes that in going back to it as the starting point of the new covenant in Christ, Zacharias anticipates Paul's teaching in Galatians. Barnes uses the occasion for a definition. Covenant among men implies equality between the parties, freedom from constraint, and freedom to decline; such a transaction can never take place between man and God, since man may not refuse what God proposes and is already bound to do all that God commands — so in Scripture the word means sometimes a command, sometimes a promise, sometimes a law, and sometimes the way in which God dispenses mercy. Here, as the following verses show, it means the promise made to Abraham.

Calvin sets out the order in which the thing happened, and insists the order matters. First, God was moved by pure mercy to make a covenant with the fathers. Second, he linked the salvation of men to his own word, so that it depends on it. Third, he exhibited every blessing in Christ, so as to ratify all his promises, whose truth is only confirmed to us when we see them fulfilled in him. Forgiveness is promised in the covenant, but it is in the blood of Christ; righteousness is promised, but offered through his atonement; life is promised, but must be sought only in his death and resurrection. He explains the word remember in the same way: there might well be some appearance of forgetfulness during that long delay in which God let his people languish under very heavy calamities. Gill takes the mercy promised to be salvation by Christ, and notes that the fathers under the Old Testament were saved by the same grace, his blood having been shed for the remission of sins that were past.

That the promise reaches backward as well as forward is Calvin's next point, and a striking one: Zacharias speaks of a mercy shown in his own generation as extending to fathers already dead, who equally shared its results. From which it follows that the grace and power of Christ are not confined within the narrow limits of this fading life but are everlasting; and as neither Abraham nor any of the saints could procure salvation by his own power or merits, the same salvation has been exhibited in Christ to all believers, whether living or dead. On the oath itself Gill recalls that God swore by himself, because he could swear by no greater, that in blessing he would bless Abraham, and that his seed should possess the gate of his enemies. Barnes points to the same passage in Genesis; Robertson notes the attraction by which the antecedent has been drawn into the case of the relative, and adds that the oppression of the Gentiles seems to have been in the speaker's mind, though it is uncertain how clearly he grasped the idea of a spiritual Israel. Calvin explains why an oath is mentioned at all: it expresses more fully the firmness and sacredness of God's truth, since he deigns to employ his own name to support our weakness — and if his bare promises do not satisfy us, and this confirmation does not remove all doubt, we are chargeable with heinous ingratitude and with insult to his holy name. Ellicott notes only that the noun stands in apposition to the covenant of the previous verse.
74:
Chrysostom points out that the verse claims two things not easily found together. Many escape danger but fail of a glorious life, like criminals discharged from prison by the king's mercy; others reap glory but must encounter dangers for its sake, as soldiers embrace an honourable life and are often in the greatest peril. The horn brings both at once, rescuing us not slightly but in a wonderful manner, so that we have no fear left. Calvin fixes on the purpose clause: the redeemed were to consecrate themselves entirely to the Author of their salvation, for as the efficient cause of salvation was the undeserved goodness of God, its final cause is that by a holy life men should glorify his name. We are redeemed at a great price, he says, not to serve the lusts of the flesh but that Christ may reign in us. Ellicott finds the Greek plainer than the English that this was the end to which the covenant and the oath had been pointing all along, the service meant being worship as well as obedience; and he notes again that the shape of the hope suggests an early date, since by the time Luke wrote there was no prospect of the Jews being delivered from earthly enemies — what was transitory in the hymn had vanished, and the words had gained the permanent sense they keep in the worship of the Church. Robertson observes that the verb for serving originally meant service for hire.

The words without fear carry more weight than they look. Calvin takes them to mean that we cannot worship God properly without composure of mind: men who are ill at ease, struggling over whether God is favourable or hostile and whether he accepts or rejects their services, may labour anxiously in worship but will never sincerely obey, since alarm and dread make them turn from him with horror. No sacrifice is acceptable which is not offered willingly and with a cheerful heart, so men must obtain peace of conscience before they can truly worship — which is why the psalm says there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. Barnes lists what the fear would be of: death, spiritual enemies, external foes. Wesley calls it slavish fear, and hears in the verse the substance of the great promise — that we shall be always holy and always happy, joyfully serving God in every thought, word and work.

The two nouns of the next verse divide the duty in the familiar way. Ellicott says holiness has special reference to man's relations with God and justice to those that connect him with his fellow men, though the words overlap; Chrysostom draws the same line and adds the point of the phrase that follows — Zacharias does not say before men, as of hypocrites desirous to please men, but before God; and not once or for a time, but all the days of their life. He notes too what kind of service is meant: not in the flesh with the blood of victims, but in the spirit with good works. Gill makes the same contrast: not mere outward rites and ceremonies but the principles of righteousness and true holiness in which the new man is created. Clarke gathers the passage into a summary of what salvation consists in: deliverance from our enemies, so that sin has neither dominion nor existence in us; the worship of God; holiness, an inward conformity to the mind of Christ, and righteousness, a full outward conformity to the precepts of the gospel; all done before God, under the continual support of his grace; and a blessedness continuing as long as we exist. What a pity, he adds, to have lived so long without God in the world, when so much happiness and glory are to be enjoyed in union with him.
76:
The song turns aside to address a week-old child, and Calvin explains the licence: Zacharias observes no prophetical endowments in an infant of eight days, but turns his eyes to the purpose of God and speaks of it as already settled, since a secret calling had taken place and it only remained that its nature be made known to men. Following the angel, he affirms that the child will be the herald of Christ. Gill notes that the words are spoken for the sake of those present rather than the infant, and presses the title: the Highest here is the Lord Jesus, whose forerunner John was, which Gill takes as proof that Christ is the most high God. Robertson observes that the word prophet is applied directly to the child, whom Jesus would afterwards call more than a prophet. Ellicott hears in the verse an echo of two prophecies at once, the going before Jehovah of Malachi and the preparing of the way from Isaiah.

Clarke works through the prediction in parts, taking it to proclaim the dignity, the employment, the doctrine and the success of the son, together with the ruin and recovery of Jews and Gentiles alike. Prophet, he says, has two acceptations — one who foretells future events, and a teacher of men in the things of God — and John was both, announcing the baptism of the Holy Spirit and teaching men how to leave their sins; even his name was a standing prediction of the salvation of God, and he had the honour of being the last and clearest prophet of the old covenant and the first of the new. As to the employment, he was to be the immediate forerunner of Christ, none being capable of succeeding him in that ministry but Christ himself. Barnes puts it more briefly: a prophet is one appointed by God to declare his will, and to go before a man's face is simply to go immediately before him.

What he was to teach is named in the next verse, and Clarke calls it the science of salvation: men are ignorant and must be instructed, and the human sciences, profitable as they may be in earthly matters, cannot profit the soul — the science which teaches God must come from God, and none is of any avail to the soul which does not bring salvation with it. Gill rules out the salvation the nation was hoping for, since John gave no intimation of deliverance from the Roman yoke, and adds that the knowledge meant is not merely notional but experimental, and is a gift rather than something acquired by industry. Ellicott says the same of the aim of the mission: men had lost sight of the true nature of salvation, being wrapt in dreams of deliverance from outward enemies, and needed teaching that it consisted in forgiveness for past sins and power to overcome sin in future. He notes too that these are historically the first words about the remission of sins in the Gospel records, and sets them beside our Lord's words at the Last Supper, since the two ministries, different as they were in outward form, agreed in this. Calvin treats the clause as the principal subject of the gospel: since we are by nature children of wrath and are chargeable with unrighteousness, there is no provision for escaping eternal death but God reconciling us to himself and not imputing our trespasses. True righteousness, he concludes, is nothing else than the imputation of righteousness, when God out of free grace acquits us from guilt — and since Zacharias is speaking not of strangers to the covenant but of the people of God, believers stand righteous before him by imputation to the very end. Wesley takes the immediate sense to be that John was to preach salvation by the remission of sins.
78:
The phrase is more physical in the Greek than in English. Ellicott renders it literally as the bowels of mercy of our God, and explains that this was how the Jews spoke of what we should call the heart of God; he insists too on the force of the preposition, since the pity that moved that heart is thought of not as the instrument through which but as that on account of which the Baptist's work was to be done. Robertson gives the same literal rendering and notes the margin's hearts of mercy. Calvin says Zacharias was not satisfied with calling this the salvation brought by Christ, but used more emphatic language and traced it to the very bowels of God. Gill spells out how far back the mercy reaches: it moved God to enter into covenant with his Son, to set him forth in the eternal purposes and to send him in the fulness of time; and whatever the pardon of our sins cost God and Christ, it is all free grace to us.

The next word has two possible senses, and three of the commentators point to the same choice. Barnes takes it for the morning light, the aurora, the rising of the sun, and explains the qualifier — it is the dayspring from on high because the light of the gospel shines out from heaven. Ellicott thinks the English word catches the Greek beautifully, the dawn being seen in the east rising upward and breaking through the darkness; but the same word had acquired a distinctly Messianic association through its use in the Septuagint for the Branch, that which springs upward, so that here a name which had become Messianic is taken in its primary sense and turned into a parable. Robertson agrees that the word can be used of a sprouting plant but says that does not suit the context. Calvin reads it as a metaphor of the great mercy of God making the day to dawn, and hears behind it Malachi's prediction, where Christ is called the Sun of Righteousness and is said to arise with healing in his wings.

Barnes turns the closing verse into a picture of travellers overtaken by night, waiting patiently for the morning that they may see which way to go: so man wandered, so he became benighted, so he sat in the shadow of death, until the Sun of righteousness arose and the road lay open before him. Ellicott hears an echo of Isaiah and carries the image further, the sunrise lighting the path of men who had sat all night in a dark ravine and whose feet are now guided into the way of peace — a word which with the Hebrews always included every form of blessedness. Robertson notes that the verb is an old one for shining upon, as the sun or stars do, and adds a sober aside: we are still on that road, though so many stumble for lack of light, men and nations alike. Gill identifies those in darkness as God's elect among the Jews, in the darkness not only of an unregenerate state but of the legal dispensation, having lost the knowledge of God's righteousness under blind guides. Calvin raises the obvious objection — how could Israelites be said to sit in darkness, when the Lord always shone on their hearts by faith? — and answers that the godly under the law were surrounded on every side by the darkness of death and saw at a distance, in the coming of Christ, the light that cheered them and kept them from being overwhelmed. He adds that peace here must carry the full Hebrew sense of every kind of prosperity, so that we may not seek the smallest portion of happiness anywhere but in Christ.
80:
The chapter closes on thirty silent years, and the commentators divide the growth between body and soul. Gill has the child growing in stature of body while increasing in wisdom and knowledge and in fortitude of soul; Clarke, increasing in stature and bodily vigour while his understanding was divinely illuminated and confirmed in the truths of God. Barnes reads the second clause as courage, understanding and purposes of good, all fitting him for his future work, and pauses over the English verb, which means simply to increase and comes from an old Saxon word. Robertson notes that both Greek verbs are imperfects, so that the sentence describes a child who kept on growing in strength of body and of spirit rather than one who had arrived at either.

Where he spent the interval is answered only in general terms. Barnes places him in Hebron and the hill country where his father had lived, dwelling in obscurity and unknown publicly to the people; Clarke adds the neighbourhood of Nazareth to the same list. Ellicott admits at once that we have no materials for filling up the outline, and then sets down what may fairly be surmised: the usual Jewish education, the observance of the Nazarite vow, the death of his parents while he was still comparatively young, an early retirement to the deserts round the western shores of the Dead Sea, study and meditation given to the Law and the Prophets, a steadfast waiting for the consolation of Israel, and possible intercourse with the Essenes of that region or with hermit-teachers like Banus, the master of Josephus, whose manner of life was after the same fashion as his own. This much is probable, he says, and we cannot say more; but whatever the surroundings, the man entered on his work in a spirit intensely personal and original.

The last phrase names the terminus. Clarke takes it of his thirtieth year, before which the law did not permit a man to enter the public ministry; Barnes reads it the same way, until he entered on the ministry recorded by Matthew, at about that age. Robertson notes that the noun for the showing occurs here alone in the New Testament, though it is found in Plutarch and Polybius, and that the related verb carries a sacrificial sense. He ends with a reflection on the two childhoods the chapter has set side by side: the boy, as he grew, may well have gone up to the passover and may even have seen the boy Jesus there, without knowing that he was to be the Messiah — so these two children of destiny grew on with the years, the one in the desert hills near Hebron after Zacharias and Elisabeth had died, the other the young carpenter up in Nazareth, each waiting for his own showing unto Israel. Gill, closing more briefly, identifies the child of the verse simply as John, the son of Zacharias and Elisabeth.
